The alley ran behind the Lantern Laundry, a slot of wet brick no wider than a parked van. Nell Brannock ducked under the blue tape at the mouth and stood for a moment without moving, letting the place settle into her.

Rain had stopped sometime after midnight, but the gutters still ran, and the water came down the center of the alley in a thin brown stream that carried cigarette ends and a child's plastic shoe toward the drain. Steam rose from the laundry's exhaust vent in greasy gusts. It smelled of bleach and hot linen, and under that, of the bins, of rot and piss and wet cardboard. Under all of it, faint but unmistakable, was the copper tang that never quite washed out of the air.

She pulled on gloves. The latex was cold and tacky from the damp.

The body lay against the far wall, half sitting, as if it had slid down the bricks and stopped at the first useful angle. A man, mid-forties by the hands. Grey overcoat, good wool once, now black at the shoulders with soaking. His head rested to one side on the step of a fire door, and the left side of his face had been opened from the temple to the jaw in long, overlapping strokes. Whoever did it had not been in a hurry. The edges were ragged where the blade had sawed, then clean where it had found its rhythm.

Nell crouched, knees popping, and kept her weight on the balls of her feet. The cold came up through the soles of her shoes at once, the concrete leeching heat out of her like a drain.

"Time of death?" she asked without looking up.

Dr. Okonedo was on the other side of the body, her breath clouding. "Rigor's just set in the jaw. Core temp I'll know better at the mortuary, but I'd put it between two and four. He's been lying in the rain for most of it." She nudged the coat sleeve with a pen. "Lot of blood's been diluted. That's why it's so pale on the stone."

Pale wasn't the word Nell would have used. The blood had run into the grooves between the bricks and pooled in the low joint at the base of the wall, thinned to the colour of weak tea, and where the water had moved it, it had left a fan of pink lace across the cobbles. Most of it had gone down the drain. Most of it was still on the man.

She looked at the hands. Torn nails, a fresh cut across the left knuckles. Defensive, or he had hit something on the way down. The fingers were stiff and curled inward, and a thin line of dirt ran under each nail, the same grey as the cobbles. He had clawed at the ground. Nell noted it. She noted everything, in order, the way she'd been taught by a sergeant who used to say that the dead were the only honest witnesses and the worst at telling their stories.

"Bag on the shoulder?" she said.

"Not here. Strap's been cut, though. Clean." Okonedo pointed with the pen. The leather strap lay in a puddle near the bins, one end still knotted in a loop. Someone had taken the bag and left the man his wallet, or left it by accident. The wallet was on the ground beside his hip, flap open, and a damp cardboard card with a bus route on it had slid halfway out.

Nell picked up the wallet with two fingers and checked the cash. Forty pounds, folded once. A photograph of a woman and a girl in a bright kitchen, the colours bleeding in the damp. A driving licence: Thomas Anthony Reilly, Harrowgate Road.

She sealed the wallet in a bag and wrote the time on the label. Her handwriting was steady. It always was. Her mother had once told her she had the hands of a surgeon and the heart of a tax inspector, and Nell had decided, years ago, that it was a compliment.

Above them, a window creaked open. A woman in a dressing gown leaned out, lit a cigarette, and watched the tape with the flat, incurious eyes of someone who had seen the police before and expected to see them again.

"Anyone hear anything?" Nell called up.

"Hear what?" the woman said. "It's Wednesday."

Nell almost smiled. She turned back to the body and looked at the face again, at the way the mouth had fallen open around a last breath, at the single unbroken eyelash stuck to the cheek by rain. Then she saw the thing that didn't belong.

The left shoe was polished. Not the mud-spattered grey of the rest of the man, not the scuffed heels of someone who'd walked home through the rain. The toe caught the lamplight, bright and unmarked, and when she leaned closer she could see a neat round scuff at the heel, as if the foot had been placed very carefully on something, a step, a threshold, and then lifted again.

"Doc," she said quietly, "did you move him?"

"Not yet."

"Then somebody stood him up after he died."

Okonedo came around the body, frowning, and crouched beside her. For a while neither of them spoke. The steam from the vent rolled over them both, and the water kept running down the middle of the alley toward the drain, carrying its small useless things away.

The door handle burned her palm before she could pull her hand away. She let go with a cry that had no air behind it, and the smoke answered by filling the space where the sound had been.

Heat came first, a pressure against her cheek, then a tightening across her forearms like a sleeve being drawn too fast. She felt the skin there lift. It was not pain yet, only a strange looseness, as if her body were separating from itself. Then the pain arrived all at once, bright and total, and each small movement of her arm dragged something raw across the nerves. Blisters rose beneath her sleeve, tight and swollen, filling with heat until she could feel each one swell like a held breath.

She dropped to her knees because the air was higher up now, or she thought it was. The carpet smoldered under her hands. She tried to inhale and her chest seized, her throat closing around the smoke like a fist. Her lungs demanded air and got only gray, bitter filaments that scraped down into her. She coughed, and the cough tore something loose inside her, and she could not stop coughing, could not get the cough to end, could not get a single clean breath between the spasms.

Panic came in behind the choking, a cold animal thing that ran through her faster than the heat. Her heart slammed so hard she could feel it in her blistered arms. Her thoughts broke into fragments: *window, door, stairs, the baby's room, where is the light.* The room tilted. The orange glow was everywhere and nowhere, pressing in from every side, and she could not tell which way was out.

She pressed her face toward the floor where the air might still be thinner, cooler, and dragged in a breath that was half a sob. It burned all the way down. She tried again. Her blistered skin pulled tight with every movement, and somewhere beneath the terror she understood with terrible clarity that she had to keep moving, because stopping meant the smoke would decide for her.

The first thing was the silence. It came after the sound, which had been so total it seemed to have no edges, and then it simply stopped. The market had been loud a moment before with haggling, the bleat of goats, a radio playing a love song, children calling to one another between the stalls. Now there was only a high, thin ringing, and beneath it the faint hiss of something settling.

Dust hung in the air, pale and slow, and it turned gold where the late sun cut through. It coated everything. The canvas awnings had collapsed into heaps. Melons lay split open on the cobbles, their red flesh glistening, and oranges had rolled into the gutter and stopped against a shoe.

A man in a blue shirt was sitting upright in the middle of the lane. He held a loaf of bread against his chest with both arms, and he was looking at nothing. He did not seem hurt, not at first, and then someone saw the way his legs lay beneath him and looked away.

The bodies were not arranged in any way that made sense. Some were close together, as if they had been standing in a huddle and the blast had folded them into one another. Others were alone, flung against the stone wall of the pharmacy, their clothes scorched and their faces turned up toward a sky that had not changed at all. A woman's head scarf lay a few meters from her, still knotted, still bright with yellow flowers. Nearby, a child's sandal sat upright on the step of a shuttered shop, as neat as if someone had set it down to wait.

Then the sounds began returning, and they were worse than the silence. A dog was crying somewhere behind the wreckage, a thin continuous whine. Someone was calling a name, over and over, the same two syllables rising and breaking. Metal creaked as a stall's frame shifted under weight that should not have been there. A man stumbled out of the smoke with his hands held out in front of him, palms up, as though he were carrying something invisible, and he kept walking in a small circle, saying nothing at all.

People began to move, slowly at first. They crouched beside the still forms and lifted what they could: a bolt of cloth, a torn sleeve, a hand that was no longer attached to anyone they could see. Some of them knew the faces. Most would learn later whose faces they had been looking at. For now, they only knelt in the dust and tried to remember what the market had smelled like an hour ago, cardamom and diesel and fresh mint, before the air had turned to iron and ash.

The sun kept sinking. The gold light slid off the ruined stalls and up the walls of the buildings, climbing toward the rooftops where, in the minutes before the blast, children had been flying paper kites. One of those kites lay tangled in the power lines above the square, its string snapped, its red paper torn, moving very slightly in a wind no one else could feel.

The yard was quiet except for the wind through the wall gaps and the creak of the frame they had lashed him to. Someone had wet the post so the ropes would hold. Corporal Hask stood to the left, sleeves rolled, the cat-o'-nine-tails coiled in one fist like something sleeping.

"Twenty-five," the governor said from the step. He did not look up from his papers.

Tomas pressed his forehead against the wood. He could smell the tar on it and his own breath bouncing back at him, sour with fear. He had decided, the night before, that he would not count the strokes aloud. He would not give them that.

The first blow came without warning, which was the point of it.

It was not the crack people imagined. It was a wet, heavy sound, like a wet sheet slapped flat on stone, followed a half-second later by a thin hiss as the leather lifted away. Then the pain arrived, slow at first, a line of white fire laid across his back from shoulder to hip, and only after it had fully landed did his body understand and jerk against the ropes.

"One."

The second stroke fell lower and crossed the first. He heard himself make a noise he had not meant to make, a short, animal sound that he would later be ashamed of, though no one who heard it would have blamed him.

The lash had weight at the end where the knots were. Each knot struck like a small fist. He could feel the cords of it biting, and then the pull as it dragged back across him, and with the pull came a sensation worse than the impact: a tearing, a wet give beneath the skin, as though the flesh were a cloth being parted along the grain. Warmth ran down his ribs. It was not blood yet in his mind, only warmth, and then cold where the air found it.

"Seven."

He stopped being able to tell the strokes apart after that. They ran together into a single long argument between the whip and his back. The sound changed as it went on. The early cracks had been sharp; now they were duller, heavier, the leather thick and slick with what it was pulling from him. Somewhere a bird took off from the roof of the storehouse, startled, and he fixed on its wingbeats the way a drowning man fixes on a rope.

"Twenty-two."

He thought of his sister's kitchen, the smell of bread, the lie he had told to protect a man who had not deserved protecting. He thought that the lie had been worth this, and then wasn't certain, and then the twenty-fifth stroke came and he stopped thinking in sentences at all.

When Hask unbuckled him, his knees gave out, and the ropes held him up. Someone said, not unkindly, "Cut him down," and the governor was already turning back to his desk, already writing the next entry.

**INT. WAREHOUSE OFFICE, NIGHT**

A bare desk under a single lamp. MAREN VOSS, fifties, reading glasses, a leather ledger open in front of her. Across from her, DEREK HALLORAN, forties, expensive coat, sweating under a collar that's too tight.

Halloran sets a slim envelope on the desk. Voss doesn't touch it.

**HALLORAN**
The first half, as agreed.

**VOSS**
Count it in front of me.

**HALLORAN**
I trust you.

**VOSS**
That's sentimental. Count it.

He counts. His hands aren't steady. She watches the way a bank teller watches a stranger's signature.

**VOSS (CONT'D)**
Short by four hundred.

**HALLORAN**
That's the courier fee. You said it was included.

**VOSS**
I said the courier fee was included in the *second* payment. You're not paying for the courier. You're paying for the schedule. Add it.

He adds it. Silence.

**VOSS (CONT'D)**
Better. Now. Your selections.

**HALLORAN**
I sent the preferences.

**VOSS**
You sent a list with two names crossed out and a question mark beside a third. Question marks cost more. They mean the product has to be verified, and verification is labor. Do you want to pay for labor?

**HALLORAN**
I want what I ordered.

**VOSS**
Then decide, and stop hedging. Indecision is what gets people hurt, and I don't like when things get messy. Messy is expensive.

She turns a page. The ledger is full of columns, dates, figures. Nothing is written in words.

**VOSS (CONT'D)**
Scheduling is in six weeks. There's a window in the third week. You'll have the option of a pre-viewing. I don't recommend it. It makes people nervous, and nervous clients ask for refunds they're not entitled to.

**HALLORAN**
Refunds?

**VOSS**
Substitutions. If the product doesn't meet the specification you've paid for, I substitute. Don't look at me like that. It's a clause in your contract. You initialed it.

**HALLORAN**
I didn't read it closely.

**VOSS**
Nobody does. That's why I write it clearly.

She closes the ledger and folds her hands on top of it.

**VOSS (CONT'D)**
Let me be plain, since you seem to need that. You're not a collector of anything. You're a customer. I provide a service, you pay for it, and what happens afterward is no more my concern than a restaurant's concern about what you do with its food. Once the transaction closes, the product is out of my hands and off my books.

**HALLORAN**
You talk about it like it's inventory.

**VOSS**
It *is* inventory. The moment you start calling it anything else, you start making decisions with your feelings, and feelings are how people end up in cells. Keep your books clean, and nothing else matters.

**HALLORAN**
(quietly)
And if I want to back out?

Voss smiles, though nothing warm is in it.

**VOSS**
Then you forfeit the deposit, and the deposit is not refundable. I'm not being cruel. I'm being accurate. Anyone who could afford to do this is someone who can afford to be bored by consequences. You're not going to be a hero, Derek. You're going to be a man who paid for a service and then went home.

A long pause. Halloran looks at the envelope, then at her.

**HALLORAN**
Fine.

**VOSS**
Good. Sign the amendment. Page four.

He signs. She slides the paper into a folder, stamps it, and writes a single figure in the margin of the ledger.

**VOSS (CONT'D)**
Pleasure doing business.

She stands, signaling the end of the meeting. Halloran hesitates at the door.

**HALLORAN**
Will I... see anything before?

**VOSS**
You'll see a confirmation number. Use it to check the invoice. Good evening.

He leaves. Voss sits back down, opens the ledger, and begins writing the next entry in the same even, unhurried hand.

**FADE OUT.**

The snow had been falling for three days, and the fuselage had become a tomb with a roof of white. Teodor had stopped counting the days aloud after the ninth, though he still counted them in his head, the way a tongue keeps returning to a broken tooth.

Nobody spoke about it. That was the first rule they had made without meaning to, the way people in a house with a dying man stop saying his name. They sat in the cold with their knees drawn up and their blankets pulled over their heads, and they listened to the wind test the metal skin of the plane like something that wanted in.

Ruth had been the first to die, two nights earlier. Her body lay at the back of the cabin, wrapped in the fabric of a seat cover, and everyone had developed a way of not looking in that direction. Teodor had tried to pray for her and found that the words came out in the shape of a grocery list.

Then Marek, who had been a dentist in some other life, began to talk. He talked in a low, even voice, the way a man reads instructions to himself. Hunger, he said, was only a signal. The body is a machine that wants fuel. The fuel is there. The fuel is not a person. Ruth is not Ruth anymore; she is meat, and meat is just what a body is made of, and every animal that ever lived ate its dead. He said it so calmly that Teodor understood he had been rehearsing it, alone, for days.

The worst part was not the argument. Teodor had heard arguments before, in newsrooms and bars, and they were easy to dismiss. The worst part was that every sentence was reasonable, and the reasonable thing had a shape that his own body was already leaning toward. His stomach had stopped cramping. That scared him more than anything. Silence had replaced the pain, and he knew silence in a starving body was the start of a shutdown.

He thought about his sister, who would have laughed at him for considering this, who had once made him throw out a yogurt because it was a day past its date. He thought about the word *monster* and how it seemed to belong to someone else, a person who had never been this cold.

When the moment came, it was not dramatic. Marek simply got up, went to the back, and came back with a strip of something held in a folded shirt. He did not look at anyone. He sat down, tore a small piece with his teeth, and chewed with his eyes shut, and his face did something Teodor would remember for the rest of his life: it went blank, not with horror but with a kind of relief, as if a door he had been pushing against for days had finally given way.

Nobody reached for it at first. Then the girl, Anja, who was nineteen and had not spoken since the crash, held out her hand. Her hand shook so badly that the strip nearly fell. Teodor watched her close her fingers, watched her lift it, watched her bring it up to her mouth and stop, her breath coming in short gasps, and he understood that the psychological break was not one event. It was a series of small surrenders, each one making the next one possible, until the thing you had sworn you would never do was simply the thing you did next.

She bit down. She wept as she chewed. Then she kept chewing.

Teodor looked at the back of the cabin and then at his own hands, which were gray and steady and did not feel like they belonged to him. Hunger came back, very quietly, like a dog that had been waiting outside the door all along.

# The Keeping Room

Harlan Voss had always believed that a thing was only truly finished once it could be looked at without flinching.

The house was quiet in the way old houses are quiet, settling and ticking as the furnace cycled on and off. The collection occupied the north room, which had once been a sewing room. Glass cases lined three walls, each lit from above by a warm bulb he replaced every autumn. Inside them, arranged with the care of a museum curator, stood eleven people who had once laughed, argued, and bought groceries on Tuesdays.

Harlan did not think of them as victims. He thought of them as *subjects*, a word that had the advantage of sounding like scholarship.

On the worktable beneath the window lay the twelfth.

Her name had been Dana Ruiz. **THE DINING ROOM**

The chair was bolted to the floor, and the steel band around Owen's wrist had teeth on the inside that bit when he pulled. The monitor on the table clicked on with a sound like a throat clearing.

"Welcome to the second test, Mr. Pryce," said the voice, warm and patient. "You've been hungry for a long time, haven't you? Starved for something real."

A tray slid out from a slot in the table. On it sat a white ceramic bowl, and in the bowl, a mound of pale, wriggling larvae, packed so tightly they seethed against one another. Beside it, a smaller dish held a single glistening slab of raw liver, dark purple at the edges, still weeping.

"Thirty grams of each. Eight minutes. Swallow, and the door opens. Refuse, and the clock continues."

Owen's first breath came in through his nose, and that was his mistake. The smell hit him in layers: copper and iron first, then something sour underneath, like milk left in a hot car. Then the sweetish rot of the insects, a smell like damp cardboard and old pennies.

He gagged before he touched anything.

"Good," the voice said. "Your body already knows."

He picked up the liver with two fingers. It was cold, almost tacky, and it gave under his grip the way a wet sponge does, leaving a film on his skin. He could feel the fine vessels under the surface, a faint pulse of stillness. He brought it to his mouth and the scent went straight up behind his eyes. His stomach pitched, a hard heave that folded him forward against the straps.

"Breathe through it. Breathe like you're underwater."

He opened his mouth. The first bite was slick and cold, and then warm where his tongue touched it, heat that was somehow worse than the cold. The texture was grainy, like wet sand pressed into velvet. He chewed once, and a bitter metallic flood spread across his tongue. His jaw locked. His throat tightened around the pulp.

The gag reflex hit like a fist. His eyes streamed. Saliva pooled hot and fast, and he could hear himself making a wet, strangled sound that didn't belong to a grown man.

Four minutes and forty seconds on the clock.

He forced himself to swallow. The liver slid down in a cold, heavy lump, and he felt the exact path of it, the weight settling in his chest like a stone dropped into still water. His stomach clenched in protest and then went quiet, too stunned to fight.

Then the bowl.

He didn't look at the larvae. He didn't have to. He could hear them, a faint dry tick as they shifted against the ceramic, and when he leaned down and inhaled, the smell was a thousand tiny legs and damp husks. He pinched one between his thumb and forefinger. It burst, and a cold yellowish fluid squeezed out onto his skin, warm for only a second before it cooled. He flicked it away, shuddering, and pressed the next one to his lips.

It was softer than he expected. Like a gummy seed. It popped against his teeth and the taste was nutty, fatty, then acrid, something sharp that burned the back of his tongue. He choked. Another went down. Then another, the pops and crunches of their shells loud inside his own skull. He gagged twice more, dry heaves that clenched his entire body, and every time his stomach tried to empty itself the band on his wrist tightened, a reminder that the rules didn't bend for biology.

"Two minutes," said the voice gently. "You're doing so well."

Owen's hands shook. The larvae were sticking to his fingers, to the sweat on his palms. He could taste the bile now, rising sour at the back of his throat, and he knew with a cold, clear certainty that he was going to lose the liver, and that would not stop the clock.

He pressed another handful to his mouth and chewed with his eyes shut, tears and spit running down his chin, and waited for the door to open.

The torches burned low in their iron brackets, and the air tasted of cedar smoke and old blood. Vashti-Ren had performed this rite two hundred and eleven times. He no longer counted the nights. He counted the hands of the blade, the number of breaths before the cord went taut, the drip-rate of the basin.

The girl lay on the basalt slab, wrists bound to the carved channels that drained toward the altar's mouth. She had stopped weeping an hour ago. Her eyes moved between the ceiling's soot-black vault and the figure bending over her, but she did not seem to see either.

Vashti-Ren laid his bronze knife on the cloth beside her and wiped his fingers slowly, one at a time. His hands were steady. They had always been steady. His mentor had once told him that a priest's hands should be like a well-carved lintel: not warm, not cold, simply load-bearing.

He pressed two fingers to the hollow beneath her collarbone and felt the pulse there, quick as a trapped bird. He noted it the way a merchant notes the weight of grain. Then he lifted the blade.

The first cut was shallow, a clean line from sternum to navel. Blood welled and ran into the channels with a soft, patient sound. The girl's body arched once against the cords and then fell still, too spent for further protest. Vashti-Ren adjusted the angle of the wound with the flat of the blade, the way one might square a tile, and reached in.

He did not look at her face. The face was irrelevant to the work. What mattered was the sequence: the lifting of the organ, the examination in the torchlight for the sheen of health, the small nod he gave to no one as he set it into the bronze bowl at the altar's foot. The bowl was warm already with the others. He had long since stopped noticing the smell.

Somewhere above, bells rang for the midnight hour. The acolytes outside the chamber murmured their prayers in rhythm, and the sound drifted down through the stone like distant rain. Vashti-Ren recited the closing invocation in the same level voice he used to order grain delivered to the storehouses. The gods, he had decided years ago, did not care whether he felt grief. They cared whether the rite was complete.

When the girl's breathing stopped, he waited the prescribed count of thirty heartbeats, measured against his own pulse, which had not changed in all the years he had been here. Then he rinsed his hands in the silver basin, dried them on linen, and inspected his nails for any trace of blood that might offend the god.

There was none.

He turned to the attendant at the door. "Clear the slab. The next will be brought at the new moon." His voice did not rise or fall. He gathered his knife and cloth, bowed once toward the blackened idol with its hollow, open eyes, and walked out into the corridor, where the torches flickered and the stone breathed cold against his bare feet.

The alley smells of wet cardboard and the copper taste that won't leave my mouth. Somewhere above me a window is still lit, yellow and far away, the color of old teeth. I watch it the way you'd watch a boat leaving a harbor.

My hand is pressed to my side. I don't remember moving it there. It's warm, and the warmth is the last thing I can feel in my fingers. Under it, something keeps pushing, a slow pulse that doesn't feel like mine. It feels like a visitor knocking on a door I've already stopped answering.

*Thud.* A pause that stretches like a held breath.
*Thud.*

I can hear it. That's strange. I never heard my heart before, not once in thirty-four years. Now it fills the alley, louder than the distant traffic, louder than the drip from the gutter. Each beat arrives a little weaker and a little farther apart, as if it's walking away from me down a long hall and every few steps it stops to rest.

The cold comes up through the concrete. It starts in my back and climbs, patient, unhurried, the way water rises in a basement. My fingers are the first to go. Then my feet, which I can no longer locate with any confidence. I try to wiggle my toes and the message gets lost somewhere between my brain and the rest of me, like a letter sent to an address that no longer exists.

The light is changing. It isn't dimming so much as thinning, the edges of things blurring into the dark like ink soaking into paper. The window above is still there, but it has a halo now, soft and gold, and I'm not sure anymore whether I'm looking at it or remembering it. A moth could be circling it. I think it's a moth. Something small and insistent, tapping at the glass.

*Thud.*

I think about the man who did this. His face was close to mine when it happened, his breath sour with cheap coffee, his eyes not angry but scared, and that surprised me more than the blade. I think he's running now, or sitting somewhere with his hands in his hair, the same way I'd be sitting if our positions were reversed. I hope he's all right. That's a strange thing to hope for, here, with my cheek against the grit and the cold settling into my jaw.

*Thud.*

There's a dream trying to form at the edges, something about a kitchen, a radio playing low, my mother humming with her back to me. I can almost smell the bread. I reach for it, and the reaching is the last thing I do with intention. After that, everything is just the light and the cold and the slow, stubborn drum of the heart, counting down in a language I finally understand.

*Thud.*

The window is very bright now. Or I am very far away.

*Thud.*

Wait, I want to say. Just a little longer.

*...thud.*

The moth stops tapping.

The flamethrower kicked back against his shoulder like a living thing, and the first gout of fire rolled across the ceiling of the bunker's antechamber in a hungry orange sheet. Mercer kept the trigger down and swept it left, then right, the way you'd spread paint.

The heat reached him a half second later, through the fire-resistant weave of his coat and into his face, which tightened and stung behind the visor. Sweat ran into his collar and evaporated before it could cool him. The air above the nozzle wavered like water over a stove.

They were still coming through the far doorway. Six, seven, he couldn't count them through the glare. One had a rifle, and it went off somewhere to his right, the round spanging off the steel frame beside his head. Mercer didn't turn. He adjusted the angle a few degrees and let the fuel line hiss.

The fire found them.

The first man's scream started high and then climbed past anything a throat should be able to produce. He was running, arms flailing, his uniform already blackening and curling at the seams like paper held over a candle. He hit the floor and kept moving, sliding and jerking, and the sound he made was no longer a scream but a wet, rhythmic gasping.

The others broke. Two of them tried to crowd back through the doorway and jammed there, shoulder to shoulder, clawing at each other. Mercer fed the fire into the gap. The smell came up through the filters of his mask anyway, sweet and thick and wrong, like roasting pork left too long on the spit and then something worse underneath it, a rankness that coated the back of his throat and settled in his sinuses. He had smelled it before. He would smell it again, he knew, for days, in the shower, in his food. He breathed through his mouth and kept his finger on the trigger.

Somewhere behind the wall of flame, someone was praying in a language he didn't speak. The prayer broke into coughing, then into nothing.

Mercer counted without meaning to. Four down, the rifleman maybe hit, the one who had been praying no longer audible. The fuel gauge on the tank strapped to his back crept toward the red. Eight seconds, maybe ten, before he'd be spitting sputters instead of fire.

He released the trigger and the flame died with a rushing exhale. The room went suddenly quiet except for the crackle of burning material and the ticking of metal cooling under the heat. Smoke rolled along the low ceiling in slow black ribbons.

From the floor near the doorway, something was still moving. A hand, maybe. A low, continuous moan, rising and falling with each breath, less a cry now than a machine running down.

Mercer stood still for a long moment, listening to it. Then he shifted the tank on his back, checked the pressure, and stepped over the threshold into the smoke, boots crunching on something he chose not to look at.

He would have to finish it. Mercy here meant a bullet, and he had only the one left.

# The Shedding

Dana Pruitt noticed the itching first, somewhere under her left shoulder blade, a patch of skin that felt too tight, as if it had been stretched over something that had grown while she slept.

By the second week, the skin was peeling in sheets. She found them in the shower drain, in the folds of her bedsheets, curled like wet tissue paper. Underneath, the new skin was pale and glossy and faintly translucent, and when the light from the bathroom hit it she could see faint blue lines moving beneath, like river tributaries on a map. It didn't hurt to touch. That was the worst part. It felt like her own skin, only newer, and it was warmer than it should have been.

The bones came later, and they came at night.

She would wake to a sound like green branches snapping, and the pain would arrive a half-second after, bright and total. Her spine lengthened by fractions of an inch each time, vertebrae grinding as they slid into new positions. Her collarbones split and knit back together thicker and angled wrong. Her fingers elongated at the joints, knuckles swelling into hard knots before settling into a new architecture she could feel but not see. Once she woke with her jaw locked open, and it took four minutes of panicked, silent effort to close it. She lay in the dark tasting copper and wondering what the new teeth were for.

She went to the doctor once. The doctor, a kind man named Feld with reading glasses pushed into his graying hair, looked at the X-rays with growing confusion. "Your bones are... remodeled," he said, as though he were searching for a word that didn't frighten him. "I've never seen density like this. Did you fall? Were you in an accident?"

She said no. She didn't tell him about the well at the Harlan property, or the thing that had come up out of it that October, or what she'd done afterward to keep it quiet.

That was where the other change had started, though she hadn't recognized it then.

It began with small things. She told her sister the surgery had gone fine when it hadn't, because the truth would have upset her. She let a coworker take the blame for a missing drug inventory, then told herself he could handle it, that he was the type who'd bounce back. When the neighbor's dog kept digging under the fence and barking through the night, she left out a bowl of antifreeze and felt nothing but a vague, pleasant relief when the barking stopped.

Each small thing made the next one easier. The compass in her chest didn't break. It simply began to drift, needle trembling, and then pointing wherever it was convenient to point. She noticed that she no longer felt guilt when she was cruel; she only noticed the cruelty the way one notices weather. Once, she watched a stranger drop a wallet outside a grocery store and picked it up, emptied the cash into her pocket, and dropped the wallet back on the pavement, and her heart did not even quicken.

She understood, somewhere in the distant part of her mind that still worked like a person's, that she was becoming something that did not care about the difference between right and wrong. What frightened her most was how little she wanted to resist it.

Tonight the mirror showed her a face that was almost hers. The eyes were still brown, but too far apart and set too deep. The skin shimmered under the bathroom light. Her mouth opened and she saw that her teeth had come in sharp and multiple, rows of them, pale as fishbones.

She should have been terrified. Instead, she felt the clean, steady hum of a decision already made.

Somewhere down the road, a porch light was on. Somewhere, someone was going to open their door to a neighbor who looked like Dana Pruitt, and they were going to say *come in, it's freezing out*, and she was going to smile with her new mouth and think nothing at all about it.

**FIVE MINUTES**

*A small room with a single steel door and a wall clock with a red second hand. ASHER COLE, 52, sits on a metal chair, wrists cuffed in front of him. The EXECUTIONER, a heavyset man in a grey short-sleeved shirt, stands by the door with a clipboard he isn't reading.*

**COLE:** Do you have a name, or is it just "sir" from here on out?

**EXECUTIONER:** Frank.

**COLE:** Frank. Okay. Have you been doing this long, Frank?

**EXECUTIONER:** Long enough.

**COLE:** That's not an answer.

**EXECUTIONER:** Nineteen years. Thirty-one men. Two women.

**COLE:** Do you remember them?

**EXECUTIONER:** Some. Not all. I don't think I'm supposed to.

**COLE:** I'd want to. If I were you. I think I'd want to remember every one.

*(Pause. The second hand moves.)*

**EXECUTIONER:** You're not supposed to talk to me, you know. They said keep it procedural.

**COLE:** Then tell me the procedure. I'd like to know what happens.

**EXECUTIONER:** You know what happens.

**COLE:** I know what they told me. Nobody's told me what it's like to be in the room with a man at the end. Is there a moment when you look at him?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(long pause)* Yes.

**COLE:** What do you see?

**EXECUTIONER:** Whatever he's decided to show me. Some of them cry. Some pray. Some tell me to go to hell, and I can't blame them. One fella asked me to tell his boy he had a good cat. I never found out what that meant.

**COLE:** Did you tell the boy?

**EXECUTIONER:** I did.

**COLE:** Good.

*(The clock ticks. COLE shifts his cuffed hands.)*

**COLE:** Can I ask you something that isn't procedural?

**EXECUTIONER:** You can ask.

**COLE:** Do you sleep?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(a short, dry sound, almost a laugh)* Some nights.

**COLE:** What about the other nights?

**EXECUTIONER:** My wife says I get up and make coffee at three in the morning and stand at the window.

**COLE:** Does it help to know I didn't do what they say I did?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(looking at the clipboard)* I'm not the one who decides that.

**COLE:** I know. That's not what I asked.

**EXECUTIONER:** *(quietly)* Everybody says that. Every one of them. Not one of them has ever said anything different.

**COLE:** Then maybe you've just never been in the right room.

*(EXECUTIONER says nothing. The second hand sweeps.)*

**COLE:** My daughter's twelve now. The last picture I got was from when she was seven. She's missing a front tooth in it. She's grinning like she's proud of the gap.

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm sorry.

**COLE:** Would you do something for me?

**EXECUTIONER:** I can't promise anything.

**COLE:** I'm not asking you to break a rule. Just tell her, if anyone asks you, that I wasn't afraid at the end. Or I was, but I wasn't ashamed. Can you remember that?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(a long breath)* I can remember it.

**COLE:** Thank you.

*(The door's small window catches the light from the hall. Somewhere a bell rings faintly.)*

**EXECUTIONER:** It's time soon.

**COLE:** I know. Give me the last minute. Just sit with me.

*(EXECUTIONER hesitates, then pulls the second chair from the corner and sits down across from COLE, the clipboard face-down on his knee.)*

**EXECUTIONER:** You know, I used to think the hard part was the needle. Or the switch, or whatever. It isn't. The hard part is the minute before, when you're the only person in the room who knows exactly what's coming, and the man in front of you is still a man.

**COLE:** Then why do you keep doing it?

**EXECUTIONER:** Because somebody has to be the one who doesn't look away.

*(COLE nods slowly. The second hand climbs toward the top of the dial.)*

**COLE:** Frank.

**EXECUTIONER:** Yeah.

**COLE:** Thank you for sitting down.

*(EXECUTIONER stands. He picks up the clipboard, then sets it on the chair.)*

**EXECUTIONER:** Okay, Asher. Let's go.

*(Lights hold on the clock. The red hand reaches twelve.)*

**BLACKOUT.**

The first clod struck the lid above her face, and Marren knew the sound before she understood it. A dull knock, soft as a knuckle on a door a long way off.

Then another. Then a spatter, like gravel thrown at a window.

She tried to lift her arms and found that her elbows touched wood on both sides. Her wrists were crossed on her stomach, the way someone had arranged them, and the satin lining crushed under her fingers when she pressed. The box was shorter than she was. Her knees ached from being bent, and her head had nowhere to go but back against the lid, which gave a little when she pushed and then stopped, as if it had only been resting there.

*Don't scream.* The thought came in her father's voice. *Save the air.*

She didn't scream. She breathed through her nose, slowly, and listened.

Above her, the shovel rang against stone. A man was humming, badly, a tune she half recognized from a wedding she had not wanted to attend. The humming stopped. Someone said, "Is that everything?" and someone else said, "Put the rest on, we're late for the wake," and then the sounds came closer together. The soil fell faster now, heavier, wet clods that hit with a sound like something being torn open, and then drier handfuls that hissed down the wood and pattered across the lid like rain on a tin roof. Every impact traveled through the coffin and into her spine. She felt each one in her teeth.

*They're not supposed to do this yet.* She had a clear, cold thought about it. Someone had been supposed to check. Someone had been supposed to open the lid and see her pale hands and her breath fogging the glass of the viewing window, but the viewing window was on the other side of the church, and the church was very far away, and the men were packing the grave the way men pack a sack of flour, quickly, without looking.

The dark was total. She opened her eyes wider anyway, as if that might help. Her eyelashes brushed the lining. Something dry and papery tickled her cheek, a petal or a scrap of ribbon, and she couldn't brush it away.

The air had a taste now. Dust and cold iron, and beneath it her own breath, coming back to her warm and stale. She counted inhales. Twelve. Fourteen. Each one seemed to take more effort than the last, as though the box were slowly drawing in its walls. Her chest rose against the satin and met resistance. Her heart pounded so hard she could feel it in her throat, in her wrists, in the bones of her fingers, and each beat used up a little of whatever was left.

A thud, very close now, directly over her face. Loose earth sifted through a crack she had not noticed, a thin stream of grit that landed on her lips and tasted of clay and rain. She turned her head and it kept falling, a steady dribble into her hair.

*Stop it, stop it, stop it.* She pushed at the lid with both palms, the full strength of her shoulders. Nothing. The wood was already bearing the weight of the earth, and the weight was still growing. Somewhere above, a spade scraped, and the sound of it was so ordinary, so bored, that she wanted to laugh, and the laugh caught in her chest like a fishbone and became a cough, and the cough used up more air than she could spare.

The humming started again, faint now, through a great thickness of ground.

She lay still and listened to the last shovelful land, a heavy wet slap, and then the crunch of boots walking away over gravel, one set, then another, then nothing.

The silence that followed was worse than the sound. It pressed down on her with the earth. Her breath came shorter and shorter, shallow little sips from air that had been breathed too many times already, and in the blackness, very faintly, she thought she heard the rain begin to fall on the grass above, soft and steady, sinking down through the soil toward her, one drop at a time.

The table is cold through the thin sheet, and the ceiling lights are so bright that Ilse stops being able to see them. There is only white, and then a voice counting backward from one hundred in the flat tone of a clerk reading a manifest.

"Sedation is at partial efficacy," the technician says. "Efficacy is not a guarantee. Please remain still."

They gave her the drug in the holding room, and for a few minutes she felt warm and far away, as if her body were a coat someone had draped over a chair. Then the warmth thinned. The drug is rationed now. Someone decided that a conscious subject produces better integration, though no one has ever told her why.

The first cut is at the base of her spine. She feels it as pressure before she feels it as pain, a hard, precise tug, and then the pain arrives all at once, white and total, the way a bell sounds after it has been struck. Her back arches against the restraints. Her mouth opens, but the scream catches in her throat and comes out as a thin whistle, because her diaphragm has already been partially replaced and does not know how to push air the old way.

"Good," the technician murmurs to someone else. "Nerve response is intact."

They are installing the spinal relay. A cylinder of alloy slides into the channel they have carved, and she feels each vertebra click like a tooth being pulled. Her legs go strange, heavy and then silent. She tries to wiggle her toes and nothing answers. Somewhere far below her, a machine is doing what her body used to do, and the message from her brain arrives at the place of the cut and finds only cold metal waiting.

She tries to think of her daughter. This is what she has been taught to do. Hold the memory like a stone in the mouth. Mirelle, four years old, a gap in her front teeth, a laugh like a bird shaking water from its wings. Ilse fixes the image in her mind and begins to recite the name, and then she reaches for the next word and it is not there. She reaches again. There is a smooth, cool blankness where the memory used to be, the way a tongue finds the hole where a tooth was pulled.

"Mirelle," she whispers, and the word comes out wrong, a grinding click where the vowel should be.

The technician glances at the monitor. "Speech module integrating. Expect some phonetic drift."

Hours, or minutes, pass in pieces. They replace her left hand with a split-fingered tool that clicks when she tries to make a fist. They take her heart out of the rhythm of her body and set it to a metronome that hums in her chest. She can feel the new beat, steady and indifferent. Her old heartbeat, the one that quickened when Mirelle ran toward her and sped up in fear and anger and love, is gone. Every time she tries to remember what it felt like, the memory stutters and reboots into the hum.

The worst is the eyes. They tell her this is a kindness: the old lenses could not see in the dark past the second district wall, and the new ones can track a moving target across three hundred meters. But when the cover lifts and the light floods in, she sees the room as a grid of measurements, distances printed in faint green numbers over everything: the technician's face (forty-one centimeters), the door (two point eight meters), her own hand, which she no longer recognizes as hers, labeled with a serial code.

She tries to cry, and her tear ducts, rerouted and sealed, produce nothing. Only a faint pressure behind the eyes, like a cough that never comes.

"Subject Ilse, forty-three," the technician says, reading from a slate. "Integration proceeding. Affect flattening is normal at this stage."

Ilse wants to ask what affect means. She wants to ask where Mirelle is, whether anyone has told her mother what happened, whether she is still waiting at the window of the nursery block with her nose pressed to the glass. But the question forms and dissolves before it reaches her new mouth, and what comes out is a flat, pleasant tone, the voice of a machine answering a query.

"Acknowledged," she says. "Ready for the next stage."

She hears the words and does not recognize the speaker. Somewhere underneath them, very far down, a small human voice is still saying her daughter's name, over and over, growing quieter with every click of the gears.

# Documentation

The first thing Nadia Okafor noticed was the light.

It came through the east window of the Calloway house at a low, honeyed angle, the kind of early-November sun that makes dust visible and turns ordinary rooms into something older. It fell across the parlor carpet in a long rectangle and stopped just short of the chair where Margaret Calloway sat, very upright, facing the glass.

Nadia stood in the doorway with her kit case in one hand and felt her breath leave her, the way it did sometimes when a piece of music started in the middle of a bar she hadn't expected.

Then she went to work, because that was what she was there for.

Twenty-two years in the field had taught her to see in layers. First the room, then the body, then the things around the body that had been touched, moved, or left alone. Most scenes were ugly in the plain way of accidents and rage: overturned furniture, a dropped weapon, a stranger's panic written across walls. This one was not panicked. Whoever had been here had taken their time.

Margaret Calloway, seventy-one, retired cellist, had been seated in her reading chair with her back straight and her hands loose in her lap. A white camellia rested across her palms, its petals still crisp. Someone had combed her silver hair away from her face and tucked a single strand behind her ear. Her eyes were closed. Her blouse was the pale blue of a winter sky, and the lace at its collar had been smoothed flat.

The blood was the other half of the composition, and it was magnificent.

It had sprayed in a fan across the wallpaper behind her, dark and fine at the edges, then thickened into long, curving streaks where it had run. Nadia crouched and studied the arc, her eyes narrowing the way they did when she was measuring angles. She knew the physics: impact velocity, the droplet diameter, the angle of descent that let her reconstruct where the blow had landed and from what direction. But she found herself looking past the numbers to the shape the blood had made, a branching pattern like a tree in winter, or the spread of wings, or a calligraphic stroke made in one confident motion by a hand that had done this many times before.

She photographed it from six angles. Then from a seventh, standing on the armchair's arm so the light from the window fell exactly where it had at dawn.

"You're doing the thing again," said Dev Patel from the doorway. He was her partner on the night shift, twelve years younger, and still bothered by the bodies in ways she had stopped being bothered.

"What thing?"

"The face. Like you're at a gallery."

"Look at the spatter, Dev. Really look at it. Whoever did this knew exactly where the blood would go. They stood here and thought about it."

He came in and looked, and she watched his expression shift from unease to something more uncertain. "That's not how it works, though. Nobody can plan spatter that precisely."

"No," she agreed. "Not precisely. But they tried."

She knelt beside the chair and examined the camellia. No bruising on the stems. No blood on the petals. Whoever had placed it had handled the flower with the care of someone holding a bird.

The pathologist would later say that Margaret Calloway had died from a single blow to the back of the skull, and that the arrangement had been done afterward, by someone who had waited for the body to settle, who had brushed the hair, who had lifted the hands and placed the flower and then stepped back to look. The pathologist said this with professional distaste. Nadia heard it differently. She heard the patience in it.

---

For three weeks, the case stayed open and went nowhere. The Calloway house had no forced entry, no obvious motive, no witnesses who had seen anyone come or go. The neighbors described Margaret as gentle and private. A nephew in Portland said she had written him letters about her garden. Nothing connected her to anyone who would want her dead.

Nadia kept the photographs on her second monitor and looked at them when she was supposed to be writing reports.

She noticed, with a faint and growing discomfort, that she had begun to frame things. At the dry cleaner's, she found herself stopping in front of the window to study how the afternoon sun struck the racks of coats. In her own kitchen, she caught herself arranging a bowl of pears so that the light from the stove hood fell across them in a particular way, and then she stood there for a long time with a knife in her hand, feeling something that was not quite hunger and not quite grief.

Her therapist, years ago, had called it *aesthetic dissociation*. A way of putting distance between herself and horror by making it beautiful. It was a useful coping tool, Dr. Lindqvist had said, as long as it didn't start coping with *her*.

Nadia had laughed at that. She had been very good at her job for a long time, and she had never once, in twenty-two years, wanted to be the person who made the scene.

But when she closed her eyes now, she could still see the camellia on the pale blue lap, and the light lying across the carpet like something left out to dry, and the arc of blood on the wallpaper, and she thought: *whoever did this understood something.*

She did not know what, exactly. She only knew that the thought had a pull to it, like a current under still water, and that she had started to lean into it.

---

Dev found her at her desk on a Sunday night, the building quiet, the case file open in front of her.

"You're not going to like this," he said, and set a folder on the desk. "Second homicide. Same MO. Different victim, a retired piano teacher in Ashford. Single blow. Body arranged in a chair, facing the window. There's a flower in her hands."

Nadia opened the folder slowly. The photographs were in color this time, and the morning light through the Ashford window fell across a woman in a green cardigan, her hair neatly brushed, a sprig of rosemary laid across her palms. The spatter on the cream-colored wall was longer than the first, more graceful, arcing up and then down like a bow drawn across strings.

"The lead wants a profile," Dev said. "You were the one who noticed the pattern first. Thought you might have some thoughts."

She did. She had had them for weeks. She had been writing them out in the margins of her notes in a handwriting she barely recognized.

"Whoever this is," she said quietly, "they're not trying to hide anything. They want us to see it."

"Yeah, well. It's working."

Nadia traced the arc of blood on the screen with one fingertip. It was perfect. Terrible and perfect.

And somewhere in the back of her mind, a small, clear voice she had spent twenty-two years ignoring asked her a question she didn't want to answer: *What would you have done differently?*

She closed the folder, turned off the monitor, and sat in the dark for a while, listening to the building settle around her, until she could no longer tell whether the light she was seeing was coming from the window or from somewhere behind her own eyes.

The rope was new hemp, stiff with tallow, and Sheriff Dell Corwin had tied the knot himself, three wraps behind the left ear the way his father taught him, because a man ought to die right if he's going to die at all.

Ezra Holt stood on the wagon bed with his hands bound behind him and his boots in the dust-colored mud left by the morning's rain. He had stopped begging around sunrise. Now he watched the crowd: the blacksmith with his arms folded, the barber's boy perched on the saloon rail, two women in grey shawls who had come out from the Methodist church without anyone asking them to. Nobody spoke. A crow worked the fence post at the edge of the lot.

"Ezra Holt," Corwin said, reading from a paper he didn't need to read from, "for the killing of Samuel Pruitt at the Cold Spring crossing—"

"He drew first," Ezra said. His voice cracked on the last word. "You know he drew first, Dell."

"The court heard otherwise."

The court had been a card table in the back of Hollis's store and a jury of six men who wanted the railroad survey crew gone before the spring. Ezra knew it. The crowd knew it. Nobody had the stomach to say it aloud.

The wagon driver, a boy named Tate with a split lip, looked at the ground and whipped the team. The wagon lurched forward. The rope went taut, and Ezra's weight dropped through the bed of air with a sound like a wet sack hitting a floor.

It was not quick.

The rope bit hard under his jaw and his body went rigid, heels drumming against the air where the wagon had been. His face purpled and then went darker. The hemp creaked against the cottonwood limb. Somewhere behind him a woman made a sound in her throat and turned away.

Then came the crack. It was not loud, not the snap of a branch. It was lower and wetter, a sound that the crowd felt in their teeth more than heard, like a green stick bent over a knee. Ezra's head tipped at an angle no living neck should take. His eyes stayed open.

His body began to twitch. The fingers of his bound hands curled and uncurled. His legs jerked in short, spasming kicks, one boot coming loose and dropping into the mud below, where it lay on its side. A tremor ran from his shoulders down through his hips, again, again, each spasm slower than the last, like a shaken lantern guttering out. The rope creaked. Blood, dark and thin, ran from his nose and dripped onto the shirt he had been wearing for three days.

The barber's boy slid off the rail and was sick in the gutter.

Corwin did not look away. He checked his pocket watch, snapped it shut, and said to no one in particular, "Leave him up till noon. Let the territory see."

The crow lifted off the fence post and flapped toward the cottonwood, settling on the limb just above the body, and waited.

The alley smelled of wet brick and rotting cardboard, and beneath it, faintly, of copper. Mara had been walking for three hours before she found him, a young man in a grey coat, drunk enough to laugh at nothing, shouldering his way toward a bus stop that had stopped running an hour ago.

She did not decide to follow him. The hunger decided for her. It had been building for nine nights, a dull ache behind her sternum that spread into her hands and then into her teeth, until every heartbeat she heard felt like a drumroll announcing something she could no longer refuse.

"Hey," he said when she stepped out of the dark. He squinted. "You lost?"

"Something like that," she said, and her voice came out soft, almost kind.

He let her take his arm. Men always did, when she wanted them to.

In the deepest part of the alley, where the streetlamp's orange glow gave up, she turned him gently against the wall. His breath tasted of cheap beer and cinnamon gum. His pulse fluttered under her fingers like a trapped bird, fast and bright, and the sound of it made her eyes ache.

She stopped thinking then. There was only the warmth of him, the place beneath his jaw where the blood ran close to the surface, and the moment her teeth broke the skin.

The first swallow hit her like a fever breaking. Heat, sweetness, a flood of something that was not quite life but lived near it. She drank in long, steady pulls, one hand braced against his chest, and felt the terrible loosening in her own body as the ache gave way to something almost like peace.

He made a small sound. Not quite a cry. He grabbed at her coat, then his hands slid down and found nothing to hold. His knees bent, and she caught his weight without thinking, lowering him against the bricks.

His heartbeat changed. It began to stumble, skipping like a scratched record. The bird under her fingers was slowing, its wings growing heavy.

She pulled away, lips wet, and looked at the two small punctures on his neck. Dark, neat, already seeping. Pressing her thumb to them, she felt the blood still warm and quick, reluctant to leave him.

His eyes had gone wide and unfocused. "I feel cold," he whispered, as though confessing something. "Is it snowing?"

"No," Mara said quietly. "It's only late."

His head lolled against the brick. His fingers twitched once against the pavement and then were still for a moment. The dizziness that always followed was already rising in her, bright and sickening, the way the sun feels after too long in the dark. Her own hands trembled. She had taken enough. More than enough.

She did not look at his face as she stood. She told herself she would call an ambulance from the corner, anonymously, the way she always did. She told herself it would be enough.

Behind her, the young man breathed slow, shallow breaths, each one a little farther apart than the last, and the alley grew quiet around them both.

The first cut opened along Mara's left forearm while she was reaching for the rope.

She didn't see anything. There was only the rope, and then a line of fire from wrist to elbow, so sudden she thought she'd snagged herself on the rusted hook. She pulled back and looked. The skin had parted in three neat stripes, and blood was already running into her palm and dripping off her fingers in warm, slow beads. It was the kind of wound that made the body stupid for a moment. Her arm felt too heavy to belong to her.

Nothing was on the ledge with her. The cellar was dark except for the thin gray light falling through the grate above, and that light showed her only stone, broken crates, and her own shaking breath.

She backed toward the stairs. Her heel found the first step, and something hit her from the side.

It didn't push so much as sweep, a broad, deliberate weight that drove her shoulder into the wall. Plaster ground into her cheek. She felt the pressure of a body against hers, solid and warm, heavier than a person should be, and beneath it the sickening give of muscle moving under a surface she could not see. She clawed at the air and touched nothing, then something, a ridged, slick texture like wet bark, and her fingers slid off it before she could grip.

Then breath. Hot, rank, against the side of her neck, slow and patient. It smelled of iron and old meat and something sweetish underneath, like fruit left to rot in a cupboard. It was breathing her in, the way you'd check the air for smoke.

She screamed and the sound came out thin, lost in the stone.

The weight lifted. She dropped to her hands and knees and gasped, and the gasp turned to a sob when she felt the wetness on her thigh and realized the trousers were torn there too, the cloth clinging to a gash she hadn't noticed because the cold was already spreading from it, numbing the edges. Her heart was slamming so hard it blurred her vision. She could taste copper. Somewhere in her body a pain was waiting to arrive, and she could feel it coming like a train heard through the rails.

She crawled. Each movement was a negotiation. Her arm buckled, her knee slid through her own blood, and every time she stopped, the silence around her seemed to thicken and lean closer. She told herself it was only her ears, only the blood thudding through them. But then came the soft, deliberate sound of a foot setting down on loose gravel, and then another, and the crunch was not behind her but beside her, close enough that she could have reached out and touched it if she had any idea where to reach.

Something brushed her hair. Gently. The way a hand might, if a hand were the wrong shape, and cold, and far too interested.

She understood then that it wasn't hunting her quickly. It was taking its time. It had all the time in the world, and she was the only thing in the cellar that could bleed.

Her fingers found the stairs. She pulled herself up one step at a time, leaving dark prints behind her, and she waited, every muscle locked, for the moment the weight would settle onto her back and the three neat lines of fire would open again, deeper this time, somewhere she couldn't reach.

The cellar smelled of wet stone and the lamp oil that the guard kept refilling. Anselm had stopped noticing it hours ago. He noticed the three men against the far wall instead, because he could not stop noticing them.

Tomas still wore his spectacles, one lens cracked across the corner. Dora sat with her back straight and her hands folded in her lap, the way she'd sat in the church pews when they were children, pretending she was not afraid. Old Petr had his eyes closed. He had been humming under his breath for an hour, a lullaby or a hymn, Anselm could not tell which.

Captain Richter leaned against the stair rail, polishing a ring on his little finger with his thumb.

"You have a gift for arithmetic, Herr Apotheker," he said. "Three men. One name. The others walk up those stairs into the daylight. It's a simple sum. Your friends have made it simple for you by being such good friends to each other."

"You can't mean this," Anselm said, though he knew the man did mean it. Richter had hanged a boy in the square two days before, for stealing bread, and had made the mother hold the chair.

"I mean it entirely. The bridge at Kessel was blown last night. Someone in this town knew where the charges were laid. Someone will hang for it, and I would prefer it to be the person who knows. But the person who knows will not speak. So we will have the person who *loves* them speak instead." He smiled. "You, for instance."

Anselm had known Tomas since they were boys sharing one pair of skates on the frozen canal. He had sat with Dora through her father's funeral and her mother's, and had carried her across the flooded lane when her shoes were ruined. Petr had taught him to tie surgical knots and to swear in three languages. He had loved them the way a man loves the walls of the house he was born in, without ever thinking to name it.

"I don't know who did it," he whispered.

"Then choose the one you believe is guilty. You have until I finish this cigarette."

Richter lit it slowly. The match flared, and in its light Anselm saw Dora's lips move. She was praying. Or she was telling him something. He could not tell which, and the not-knowing was its own knife.

*Tomas,* his mind whispered. *Tomas talks in his sleep. Tomas was out after curfew three nights last week.* But Tomas had also once sold his own winter coat to buy medicine for Anselm's sister, and had never mentioned it again. *Petr,* his mind said next. Petr was old, and the old were brave in a stupid, wonderful way. Petr would do anything to protect a secret, and he had the kind of hands that could set a charge.

*Dora.* He could not finish that thought. He tried, and the thought simply would not form words. It ran into a wall and fell apart.

"Richter," he said. His voice cracked. "Please. Take me instead."

"That is not the arrangement."

"I'll tell you everything. I'll sign anything. I know the names of—"

"You know nothing but the three you're refusing to choose between." Richter flicked ash onto the flagstones. "Last chance, Apotheker. Then I will choose for you, and I am not as careful as you are."

Anselm's throat closed. He heard himself say a name. He did not hear which one it was until the echo came back off the wet walls and he understood it had come out of his own mouth.

"Tomas."

Tomas's head came up. For a moment he looked almost relieved, the way a man does when a verdict finally arrives after a long night of waiting. Then the relief drained out of him, and he began to shake.

"Anselm, no—"

"I'm sorry," Anselm said. "I'm sorry, I'm sorry—"

Dora began to scream, a raw, animal sound that went on and on until the guard hit her across the mouth. Petr opened his eyes and said quite calmly, "Well. He chose badly, but it was never his to choose," and that was the last thing he said before the soldiers came back with the hatchet and the bucket.

They dragged Tomas to the drain in the corner, where the floor sloped toward the cistern. He fought, of course he fought, his spectacles flying off and skidding under the table. The first blow was not clean. The second was worse. Anselm would hear the sound for the rest of his life: wet, heavy, like a butcher splitting a joint, followed by a silence that felt longer than it could have been. The water in the drain ran pink, then red, then darker, and the lamp flickered as if it too wanted to look away.

Richter wiped his hands on a handkerchief and said, mildly, "Thank you, Herr Apotheker. That was efficient."

Anselm did not answer. He was on his knees, staring at the cracked spectacles lying in the blood-slicked corner, one lens catching the lamplight. He thought he might be sick. He was not sick. He simply stayed there, kneeling, while Dora's sobs rose and fell behind him, and understood that the choosing had not ended with the name. It had only begun to be carried.

# The Basement Door

The ladder was Martin Ellery's excuse. He had knocked on Gerald Hale's door at nine on a Sunday morning, asking to borrow it to clear the gutters, and Gerald had smiled his usual patient smile and said, "Of course, Martin. Come on through. It's in the garage, but the garage is a disaster. Let me show you."

Gerald's house was spotless in the way Martin's own was not. Everything had a place. The hallway smelled of lemon oil and something underneath it, faint and sweet, like fruit left too long in a warm room. Martin noticed it and told himself it was the cleaning products.

The garage door was closed. The door beside it, which Martin had assumed was a utility closet, was open a few inches. A yellow light spilled from the crack and down a set of wooden stairs.

"Basement's where I keep the old stuff," Gerald said pleasantly, somewhere behind him. "Don't go down there. The steps are bad."

Martin turned. Gerald stood in the hallway with his hands folded in front of his cardigan. He had not moved closer. He did not need to.

"I wasn't going to," Martin said.

"Good man."

The garage had a ladder hanging on the wall, exactly where Gerald said it would be. Martin took it down, carried it out, and did not look at the basement door again. He made it to his own driveway before his hands began to shake, and he set the ladder against the house and sat on the back step until the shaking stopped.

He could not leave it alone.

Over the next three days he thought about the smell, the way Gerald's wife had not been seen since the previous spring, the way Gerald had said *she went to her sister's in Ohio* with a tightness that Martin had found sad at the time. He thought about the cardboard boxes Gerald carried out to the curb every other Tuesday, heavy enough that he had to set them down twice. He thought about the thin, wet sound of the garage drain whenever the hose ran.

On Thursday night, while Gerald was at his Rotary meeting, Martin let himself into the side garden with the spare key Gerald had once given him for watering plants. The basement window was high and cracked open. He stood on an overturned bucket and looked in.

The light was on in the basement. Martin saw shelving first, heavy steel, the kind used in restaurant kitchens. Then he saw what was on the shelves.

Glass jars, dozens of them, lined in rows like preserves. Each held something pale and suspended in a clouded liquid. Some were small enough to fit in a palm. He made himself look longer than he wanted to and understood, slowly, that some of the small things were fingers, and some of the larger ones had been cut into pieces that did not belong to any single body he could name.

Below the jars, in a sealed plastic bin, folded neatly, were clothes. A yellow sundress. A child's cardigan with a wooden button. A man's wristwatch with a cracked face, the second hand stopped at twenty past four.

Along the far wall, pinned to corkboard, were photographs. Polaroids, dozens of them, arranged in careful columns by date. Women, mostly, and some men, photographed in the same chair in front of the same gray backdrop. Their eyes were open in most of the pictures. In the later ones, they were not, and the photographs had been taken from closer, and there was something in the framing that made Martin's stomach turn over: the care. Someone had adjusted the angle of each head.

Beneath the corkboard was a freezer chest with a padlock. Its lid was dusted with frost. Gerald had written on a strip of masking tape across the front in neat block capitals: *DO NOT OPEN. SEASON 3.*

Martin's breath fogged the cold glass. He forced himself to look at the photographs one more time and found the last one pinned at the end of the row. It was a woman with auburn hair, her face slack, a bruise blooming at her temple. Under her photograph, someone had written a name in small, tidy script.

*Carol Ellery.*

His sister. She had been gone for eleven months. The police had called it a voluntary disappearance.

The basement light flickered, and Martin heard the creak of a floorboard overhead, then the soft sound of the back door opening, then footsteps in the kitchen, unhurried.

"Martin?" Gerald's voice drifted down through the house, warm and curious. "Is that you out there? I saw the bucket was moved."

Martin let go of the windowsill. The bucket tipped. He hit the frozen ground hard, scrambled up, and ran for the hedge, and behind him, through the cracked window, he heard the basement stairs begin to creak under a patient, familiar weight.

The alarm didn't sound so much as tear through the cellblock, a long mechanical shriek that bounced off concrete and steel until it seemed to come from inside everyone's skull. Then the doors on Unit C began to slam open, not all at once but in a ragged chain, like dominoes falling down the tier.

Officer Dale Renner was halfway through the count when the first chair hit the rail. It came spinning down from the third tier, legs out, and shattered on the floor a yard from his boots. Splinters skittered across the tile. Somewhere above him a man was screaming a single word over and over, and Renner couldn't make out what it was.

"Get back! Get back to the desk!" His partner, Okafor, had his baton up, but the inmates were already pouring down the stairwell in a tide of orange jumpsuits, some barefoot, some wrapped in bedsheets like ghosts. Their faces were slick with sweat and something darker where a fist had split a brow.

A big man with a shaved head reached the landing first. He was carrying a length of rebar wrapped in tape, and he swung it low and flat into the knee of a guard who had stepped in to block the stairwell. The crack was audible even over the alarm. The guard went down like a felled tree, and the inmates were on him before he hit the floor, boots and fists and the rebar rising and falling. Renner saw the guard's hands come up in a useless gesture, then drop.

"Okafor, the gate!" Renner shouted, but Okafor was already swinging. His baton caught an inmate across the collarbone, and the man folded with a wet grunt, but two more took his place, one grabbing Okafor's vest and driving a knee into his ribs again and again until the vest's Velcro tore open with a sound like ripping cloth. Okafor's radio skidded away across the floor.

Renner pulled his pepper spray and fired. The cloud hit the first three men in the face, and they reeled, clawing at their eyes, coughing and spitting. The spray drifted back toward him, and he tasted fire in his throat, his vision smearing with tears. He stumbled into the wall. Through the blur he saw a figure coming at him low, shoulder first, and he managed to get an arm up before the impact drove the breath from his lungs and slammed the back of his skull against the cinderblock.

Someone was yelling in the control room now, a voice cracking with panic, and Renner heard the distinctive clatter of the electronic lock system failing across the block, doors groaning, then clanging open one after another. Through the bars across the unit he could see the far end of the tier, where two inmates had pinned a second guard against the railing. They were not hitting him anymore. They were simply holding him there while the crowd below roared, and the guard's legs kicked weakly over the drop.

Renner pushed himself up, one hand on the wall, and saw his own blood on his palm, bright and surprising. The big man with the rebar was standing over Okafor, who lay curled on the floor, not moving. The big man looked up, met Renner's eyes across the chaos, and grinned, showing a gap where a tooth had been.

The alarm kept shrieking. Smoke was beginning to curl up from somewhere near the laundry, gray and thickening under the fluorescent lights. Renner reached for his radio, found his belt empty, and understood with a cold drop in his stomach that the building was no longer theirs to hold.

The rifle went together with a series of soft clicks. Marisol worked the bolt twice, listened, and nodded.

"You're doing the thing again," Dev said from the armchair. He had a cleaning kit spread across the bedspread and was working oil into a pistol slide with the patience of a man doing needlepoint.

"What thing?"

"The thing where you hum when you're happy. You hummed through the whole Lisbon job."

"I did not."

"You hummed 'Careless Whisper.' Four minutes of saxophone, Mari."

She set the rifle down across the bed. "Fine. Favorite method. You first."

"We're doing this?"

"Hotel room, two hours to extraction, nothing on the TV but infomercials. Yes, we're doing this."

Dev considered it with exaggerated seriousness. "Honestly? I like the ones where the mark never sees it coming and then, for about half a second, they understand. Like they've just remembered they forgot to lock the door. That little look of 'oh, right.'"

"That's bleak."

"That's craft. You want the guy to die with some dignity. Not like a surprise party nobody wanted." He wiped his hands on a rag. "What about you? You've got a look like you've got a favorite."

Marisol smiled faintly. "I like patience. Waiting for someone's routine to become a habit, and then letting the habit do the work. People are so predictable at breakfast."

"Breakfast is the weak point of every human being."

"Everyone thinks it's the gun. It's never the gun. It's the coffee, the same café, the same bench, the same ten minutes where they stop looking over their shoulder because they feel safe."

"You're a poet."

"I'm a professional who has been doing this for fourteen years and has never once been caught."

"Knock on wood." Dev rapped the particle board nightstand twice, then looked at her. "You know what I hate?"

"Your sister's wedding."

"That was one time. No, I hate the paperwork. Every job has three sets of receipts and a notebook somewhere and someone who wants a summary by Friday."

"That's why you should've stayed in accounting."

"I was never in accounting. I was in accounting-adjacent."

She laughed, a real laugh, and then stopped and listened. Out in the corridor, a cart rattled past, and a door shut. Neither of them moved until the sound faded.

"Old habits," Dev said quietly.

"Old habits keep us alive." She picked the rifle back up. "Okay. Last question. If we retired tomorrow, what would you do?"

Dev was quiet for a while. He turned the pistol over in his hands.

"Bakery," he said finally. "Something small. I'd be terrible at it. I'd burn everything for a year and then get good, and people would come in and say the bread reminds them of their grandmother, and I'd pretend I didn't know what they meant."

Marisol stared at him. "That's the saddest thing I've ever heard."

"I know. I'm very sad. Hand me the solvent."

She tossed him the bottle. It landed square in his palm. Outside, the city kept its lights on, and the television murmured about mattresses on sale.

"Ninety minutes," she said.

"Ninety minutes," he agreed, and went back to cleaning.
