The first thing is the wood. It was green, so it hissed and wept sap before it caught, and the smoke came first, thick and yellow-grey, rolling up into her face and filling her throat so she couldn't tell whether she was coughing or still trying to speak the prayer she had been given. Her eyes streamed. The crowd beyond the smoke became a smear of colour and shouting.

Then the heat arrived, not all at once but climbing, like water rising in a well. It found her feet first, through the thin soles of her shoes, and then her shins through her skirts. She thought distantly that she had never understood the word *scorch* until now. It was a sound as much as a feeling, a crackle that seemed to come from inside her own flesh.

She screamed when the fire reached her thighs. It was not a word, not a prayer. It was the oldest sound a body makes, pulled out of her by something no argument could reach. She heard it leave her and did not recognise her own voice.

Somewhere in it she tried to say their names, her daughter's and her husband's, but the air had gone to ash and the names came out broken, and she could not tell whether anyone in the crowd heard them. The magistrate stood with his hands folded. A child near the front was crying, and someone was telling it to hush.

Her screams climbed and tore and thinned. Near the end they were no longer screams but a hoarse, rasping breath, and then only the fire, loud and indifferent, eating the wood and the rope and all the claims that had been made about her, until there was nothing left in the square but heat, grey smoke drifting over the rooftops, and the smell that people would later pretend they did not remember.

The plague pit had been dug in the wet months, and the rain had been kind to nothing. Ysolde knelt at its lip with her sleeves pinned back to the elbow and her forearms painted with black ink that did not dry. Below her, two hundred bodies lay in tiers, row over row, like loaves set to rise in some blasphemous oven.

They had been soldiers once. Then they had been carrion for three weeks in the June heat, and the rot had done what rot does. Skin had slipped from muscle like wet paper. Bellies had swollen and split. The smell came up in a warm, sweet wall that she breathed through her teeth, because breathing through her nose had stopped being bearable at the first body and had not, in the hours since, become any easier.

"Begin," said the man behind her. Master Corvin never raised his voice. He did not need to. The dead listened to him the way dogs listen to the one who feeds them.

She laid her palm on the nearest corpse. The skin gave under her hand, cool and tacky, and a bubble of gas shifted beneath it with a soft, obscene sigh. She had expected the cold. She had not expected the *wrongness*, which came up through her fingers like a struck bell that rang a note just off true, a note that set her teeth on edge and made the candle flames lean away from it.

She began the words.

Magic, in the schools, was supposed to flow the way water flows: downhill, following the grain of the world. This did not flow. It *climbed*. It went against every law she had been taught, dragging itself up from the bottom of the pit the way a drowned man claws up a riverbank, and where it passed, things moved in ways they should not. The corpse's left arm lifted, but not at the shoulder. It bent at the elbow, then the wrist, then the fingers, each joint folding in a sequence that made no anatomical sense, as though the arm were being *unwritten* and rewritten backward. The sound it made was the sound of wet cloth being torn very slowly.

Ysolde kept her hand on the thing's chest and felt its heart, which had been still for twenty days, begin to knock. Not beat. Knock. Like a fist on a locked door from the far side.

"Good," Corvin murmured. "Now the eyes."

The eyes were the worst. They were already clouded and sunk, and when the magic reached them the lids drew back, slowly, as if lifted by invisible thread. Beneath them the eyeballs were not white. They were the color of the inside of a mussel shell, shifting, and they turned toward her with a terrible slowness that suggested not sight but *attention*. The thing was not looking at her. It was counting her. She could feel the tally in the air, a dry rattle, like beads on a string being moved one by one.

*Four. Five. Six.*

She did not know who was counting, or what, and she did not want to know.

Around the pit, the rest began to answer. Two hundred hearts knocking, out of time with one another, a noise like a hailstorm on a tin roof. Limbs twitched. A jaw dropped and hung, and from it came a low sound that was almost a word, though the language was not one spoken by anyone living. Fingers scrabbled at the packed clay of the pit walls, and the clay, where it was touched, went briefly the color of old bone.

"Too fast," she said through her teeth. "We are pulling them up too fast. Something is still *attached*."

"Something always is." Corvin's footsteps came around the lip of the pit, unhurried, and she heard him crouch beside her. When she glanced at him, his face was calm, almost gentle, which frightened her more than the dead did. He had seen what the magic cost. He simply did not count the cost as his. "The army needs bodies that stand, Ysolde. Not bodies that are at peace."

Below, the first of them stood.

It rose in one motion, too smoothly, the way no living thing ever moves. Its head turned on its neck with a sound like a green branch snapping, and it looked up at the two of them with those shell-colored eyes, and its mouth opened, and from its throat came a sound she would hear in her sleep for the rest of her life. It was not a scream. It was the sound of something being *refused*, pushed back through a door it had only just walked out of.

Then it began to climb.

Its fingers found purchase in the clay. Its knees, bending the wrong way, found the wall. Behind it, another rose, and another, until the whole pit was a slow, wet ascent of the dead, a tide of grey and green and black rising toward the light, and every step they took left a smear of dark fluid and a faint smell of something sweeter than rot, something like lilies left too long in a locked room.

Corvin stood and brushed the dirt from his knees.

"There," he said softly. "Now they will remember what they were for."

Ysolde did not answer. She was counting, too, under her breath, and she had lost track somewhere past two hundred, and she could no longer tell whether the number she heard was coming from her own mouth or from the thing that was learning, one by one, to count with her.

The stairwell smelled like bleach and old cigarettes. Marcus stood in the middle of the landing with his hands open at his sides, because Cruz had told him that closed fists looked like fear.

"Breathe," Cruz said. He was leaning against the rail, polishing a ring on his shirt. "You've been waiting two years for this. Don't look like you're going to puke."

Three others stood on the steps above. Nobody said his name anymore. They called him "the new one," even though he'd been running errands for them since he was fourteen.

The man on the floor was Eddie Ruiz, who ran a corner store two blocks over and had stopped paying. He was on his knees with his hands taped behind him, his face already swollen. He'd stopped begging an hour ago. Now he just watched Marcus, and that was worse.

"Eddie's been disrespecting us," Cruz said. "Maybe he thinks his kids make him untouchable. Maybe he thinks we forgot. You know what we don't forget?"

"Loyalty," Marcus said. His voice came out thin.

"Louder."

"Loyalty."

"Then show me."

Marcus had rehearsed this moment in his head so many times that it felt like a movie he'd already watched. In the movie, he was brave. In the movie, his hands didn't shake. Now the only thing he could hear was the hum of the fluorescent light and Eddie's ragged breathing.

"He's got a daughter," Marcus said quietly, mostly to himself.

The stairwell went silent. Then Cruz laughed, short and sharp. "Yeah? Yours had a father too, once. Doesn't matter. You want in or you want to walk out and find out what happens to people who quit?"

He didn't say what happened. He didn't have to. Marcus had seen it: a kid who left last spring, who now couldn't go to the corner without someone stepping out of a car.

Cruz held out a steel bat, dull with use. "Your move."

Marcus took it. It was heavier than he expected. His arms trembled. Eddie lifted his head and looked at him, and for a second Marcus saw the man as a person, not a problem to solve: gray at the temples, a cracked wedding band, a split lip.

"Please," Eddie said. It was the first word he'd said in a while. "Son, please. Think about—"

"Do it," one of the men on the steps said. "Or we'll do it, and you'll watch."

Marcus's throat closed. He understood, with awful clarity, that there was no version of this where he walked away clean. If he didn't swing, they would make him pay in a different way, and Eddie would still be on the floor. If he did swing, he would carry it for the rest of his life. Every choice he had left led to the same place.

He lifted the bat.

He would remember the sound for years, and he would never be able to describe it to anyone. He would remember how fast it happened, and how long it felt. He would remember Cruz clapping him on the shoulder afterward and calling him "one of us," and how the words landed like a weight he'd have to carry up and down those stairs forever.

Eddie didn't get up. Someone whistled low. Cruz was already on his phone, telling someone the job was done.

Marcus stood with the bat hanging from his hand, staring at the floor, and realized that the initiation hadn't made him one of them. It had only made him the one who could never leave.

**The Second Helping**

Margaret always took the first bite of anything new with her eyes closed, as though the food might confess something. Tonight she chewed slowly, nodded, and said, "Lamb. You've been practicing."

"Twenty years of practice," I said. "You just never noticed."

She laughed, and I watched the laugh travel through her. It started in the shoulders, loosened the knot she always carries there, and reached her throat a beat late. She reached for her wine. Her hand found the glass on the first try, which was good. Her grip was steady. There was a delay of perhaps half a second before she lifted it, as if the message had to be relayed twice.

"Do you remember the Pruitts?" she asked. "Their terrible dog?"

"The one that ate the Christmas ham."

"The whole ham, Edward. Bone and all." She set the glass down. Her fingertips tapped the tablecloth, one, two, three, then stopped, as if she'd forgotten the rhythm.

I kept my voice easy. Easy was the whole art of it. "Are you all right? You've gone a little pale."

"It's the heat in here. You always keep the fire too high." She pressed her palm flat against the linen. Her skin had taken on a faint sheen at the hairline, a dampness I knew was not from the fire. I had lit it low, deliberately. I know how a room feels when it's been arranged.

She picked up her knife again. Her hand trembled, a fine tremor that she tried to hide by sawing at the meat, and the knife squealed against the plate. She glanced up at me with a flash of irritation, the same look she has given me for thirty-one years whenever I've been clumsy at a dinner party. It was almost fond. Then the irritation slid off her face, and what replaced it was confusion, a child's puzzlement, as if someone had moved the furniture while she wasn't looking.

"Edward," she said. "The lights."

"They're fine."

"They're doubling." She blinked, slowly, then again, as though she could wipe the second candle flame away. "Everything's doubling."

I did not get up. I did not reach for her. I had decided long ago that I would not touch her until it was over, because touching would make it mine in a way I did not want. I simply watched, the way one watches a tide come in across the sand, knowing it will arrive whether or not one moves.

Her breathing changed. It became shallow and quick, high in the chest, and she pressed a hand to her sternum as though to hold something in. "My heart," she said, but the words came out slurred at the edges, soft consonants swallowed. "It's going very fast. Like a bird. Like a bird in a box."

"Try to breathe slowly," I said. The advice was useless and we both knew it. I said it anyway, because I wanted to hear my own voice being kind.

She tried to stand. Her legs did not agree. Her chair scraped back and she caught the edge of the table, and the candles shivered, and a drop of wine spilled across the cloth like a slow red bloom. She stared at it, fascinated, and I saw that she could not quite understand why it was spreading.

"I don't feel well," she said, with great precision, as if the words were a foreign language she had studied hard. Then, more quietly, looking at me with a clarity that was almost worse than the confusion: "You made the sauce."

"I did."

"You always make the sauce." A breath, ragged. "You always did."

Her hand slid down the table's edge. Her wedding ring caught the candlelight and held it. I thought of the day she had put it on, how her fingers had shaken then too, though for a happier reason.

"Edward." Her voice had gone thin, far away, like a radio station drifting out of range. "Why is it so cold?"

The fire was roaring. I had built it myself.

"Sit down, Margaret," I said. "Please."

She did not sit. She sank, slowly, back into her chair, the way a tired swimmer finally stops fighting the current. Her head tipped toward her shoulder. Her eyes stayed open, fixed on something past my left ear, and I knew without turning that there was nothing there but the wall and the painting of the harbor she had always hated.

The clock on the sideboard ticked. Somewhere in the house the refrigerator hummed, a small domestic sound, and it occurred to me that I had never noticed how loud it was.

I picked up my fork. The lamb was cooling on the plate, its fat gone white at the edges. I cut a small piece, the way I always had, and I ate it.

It was very good. She was right. I had been practicing.

The sun had not yet cleared the horizon when the crew of the *Sable Wren* were called to the main deck. No one needed to be told why. They stood in a ragged half-ring along the rail, hands clenched and eyes down, while the mutineer was dragged up from the hold.

Tobias Hale was nineteen. Two days earlier he had been among the men who tried to seize the ship's stores and lock Captain Rourke in his cabin. The attempt had failed by the length of a single breath. Now his wrists were bound behind him with tarred rope, and his bare feet slid on the wet planks as the bosun's mates hauled him forward.

"Please," he said. It came out as a croak. He tried again. "Captain, please. I was following Brannock. I didn't—"

"You followed," said Rourke. He did not raise his voice. He sat on an overturned water cask, one boot on the rail, a pistol resting on his knee as though it were a book he had finished reading. "And you chose. Stand him up."

They pushed Tobias to the gangway. The plank had been rigged over the side, its far end projecting into the air above the glittering water. Below, the Caribbean moved in slow, clear swells. Tobias could see his own reflection wavering on the surface, and then he could see what was beneath it: long grey shapes drifting in the green depths, circling with lazy patience. Three. Then five. The crew had been feeding them for two days, tossing salt pork and bone over the side, and now the sharks knew the ship the way a dog knows a dinner bell.

Tobias's knees gave out. The bosun's mate hauled him upright by his collar.

"I can't swim," Tobias whispered. Nobody answered him. Somebody at the rail began to cry quietly, and was hushed.

"Walk," said Rourke.

# The Weight of Water

The bathtub has been running for three days. I haven't touched the tap. I keep telling myself that, and I keep checking anyway, and every time I open the bathroom door the water is at the same level, just under the rim, perfectly still, and the mirror above it is fogged from the inside.

He's in the mirror now. Not in the glass, behind it, the way you'd see someone standing in a room you're not looking at. Daniel. I put the hand towel over the mirror on the first night. On the second night the towel was folded neatly on the closed toilet lid, and it was damp.

The cellar was the worst part. I did what I did down there, under the bulb with the cracked shade, and I told myself the concrete would keep it quiet. It did. The concrete has kept everything quiet. What it didn't keep was the sound.

Now I hear it in the walls. A slow drip, then a second drip that doesn't match the first, a cadence like someone counting. Sometimes it's in the pipes. Sometimes it's a cough, wet and rattling, from somewhere just behind the plaster, and I stand in the hallway with my palms flat against the wall, feeling for a pulse, and the wallpaper is warm and faintly, sickeningly soft.

At night he uses my mother's voice.

*Mara. Mara, sweetheart, come down and let me see you.* Her voice, the way she used to call me in for supper. I was eight when she died and I haven't heard her voice in twenty years, and I've never heard anyone sound so exactly like her as the thing under my bed does. It has her warmth. It also has the bubbling vowels of a throat full of river water.

I don't sleep. When I close my eyes I see the photo he kept in his wallet, the one of his daughter on a swing, and then the picture rearranges itself, and the child is standing in my bedroom doorway with her hair plastered flat to her skull and water running from her sleeves onto my carpet, and she's looking at me the way a stranger would. Politely. Waiting.

*You didn't finish,* she says, and her mouth doesn't move.

Last night I counted the fingers on my left hand four separate times, and each time I got a different number. Five. Six. Five again. This morning there was a smear of grey silt in the creases of my knuckles, though I'd scrubbed my hands raw in the kitchen sink until the skin split. I held my hand under the lamp and the silt was moving, very slowly, the way mud crawls down a windowpane.

I went to the police station last week. I got as far as the front steps. Through the glass doors I could see the desk sergeant laughing at something on his phone, and I thought, *He'll look up, and I'll say it, and it'll be over.* Instead I turned around and walked home, and the whole way back I could feel the cold coming off the river beside me, pacing me, matching my steps.

The tub is still running. I can hear it now, even from the bed, a steady hush like breath through teeth. There's a sound beneath it: slow, heavy footsteps on tile, wet and deliberate, coming down the hall toward my door. They stop. The handle turns with a soft, patient click.

I don't get up. I don't say anything. I pull the blanket over my head and I count the drips, and I lose count, and I start again from one, because I know the number matters, because he's been waiting in the water for longer than I've been alive, and he has all the time in the world to finish what I started.

The alley behind the Majestic Hotel smelled like the rest of the city: wet brick, diesel, and something sweeter underneath that had been left out too long, like fruit forgotten at the bottom of a crate.

Her name was Lorraine Pike, according to the purse someone had emptied across the cobbles. Thirty-one. Once she'd been the kind of pretty this town sold by the pound to men who could afford it and didn't ask what it cost. Now the town was collecting its debts.

Somebody had done a job on her. Not a quick one. Whoever it was had taken their time, the way a landlord takes his time evicting a family, enjoying the paperwork. I crouched beside her, my knees complaining like old pipes, and the rain came down in the thin, mean way it does in October, as if the sky had given up trying to be clean.

I've seen a lot of dead people. You stop counting after the first hundred, the way you stop hearing the el train that rattles your window every night. But you never stop noticing the silence they leave behind, that particular hush of a thing that used to be a person and is now just a room with the lights off.

Lorraine's eyes were open. They stared up past the fire escapes, past the laundry lines sagging with gray shirts, past the water tower with its peeling letters, straight into a sky the color of a bruise going yellow at the edges. Somebody should close them. Nobody ever does. The city doesn't have time for courtesy.

I thought about the streets this woman had walked. Every block in this town is a little more rotten than the last. The sidewalks crack like old teeth. The gutters choke on cigarette butts and nickel bags and the sweet-sour runoff of a hundred bakeries nobody remembers opening. The whole place is a body that forgot how to heal itself, and we're just the flies that have learned to make a living off the wound.

A cop's flashlight swept across the wall behind her, and for a second the graffiti jumped out, a crude red heart with a knife through it, the paint already flaking like dead skin. Someone had written a name inside the heart. Not hers.

Interesting.

I stood up, feeling every one of my years settle into my joints like silt in a riverbed. The neon from the bar across the street bled pink onto the puddles, a sickly infection in the water. Somewhere a siren wound up, then gave out, the way the city gives out on everybody eventually.

I took out my notebook. The pencil was short and blunt, like my patience. Lorraine Pike was going to have a lot of people asking questions about her, and most of them were going to lie, because that's what this place does to the truth. It chews it up and spits out whatever's convenient.

But the dead don't lie. They just wait for someone stubborn enough to listen.

I looked at her one more time, then reached down and gently closed her eyes.

Someone had to do it. Might as well be me.

results.model_response:
# The Quarry Hours

The rain over the Thornwood Preserve had stopped an hour before, but the trees still dripped, and every drop sounded to Mara like a footstep.

She had been running for four hours and nineteen minutes. The Ledger display on her wrist, the one the Commission had fitted during intake, still counted down in soft green numerals: *00:41:12 remaining.* Forty-one minutes until the horn, and she would be a winner, or at least a survivor, which in the Commission's vocabulary was the same thing. Forty-one minutes was a lifetime. She had stopped believing in lifetimes somewhere around hour two.

Her lungs burned. Her left shoe had split along the sole, and every step sent a sharp, hot message up her shin. She stopped behind a fallen oak, pressed her back to the bark, and listened.

Nothing. Then, far to the east, the low, rising whistle of a hunting call, two notes, the signature of Corvin Vale. Everyone in the Commission's broadcast knew that whistle. Vale was the most-watched hunter in the Reach. His sponsors paid for the whistle the way other people paid for perfume.

*He's not hunting me to win,* she thought. *He's hunting me because I'm the one the crowd is betting against.*

She ran.

---

She heard the dogs before she saw the clearing, the mechanical ones with their gleaming ribs, bred to track heat and fear. Their sensors chirped as they found her scent, and she cut left, down the slope toward the old rail bed, where the ground was soft and the ferns grew high enough to hide a body.

The ferns didn't help. The drone overhead caught her silhouette against the pale sky, and a red ring bloomed on the canopy above her. A voice boomed through the valley, warm and amplified and delighted.

"There she is, folks! Forty-one minutes on the clock, and she's still got fight in her!"

Mara didn't look up. She had learned that much from the replays.

She reached the rail bed. It was a mistake. The rails were slick, and her split shoe skidded out from under her, and she went down hard on one hip, rolling into a shallow drainage ditch. Water filled her mouth. She came up coughing, and that was when she saw him standing on the embankment above her, one boot on a fallen trunk, a rifle that wasn't a rifle slung loosely across his back.

Corvin Vale was younger than she'd expected. His face was calm, almost bored. He had the kind of stillness that came from knowing exactly how the next minute would unfold.

"You made it farther than the odds said you would," he called down, almost kindly. "That counts for something. Not much, but something."

She scrambled backward through the mud. "Please."

He tilted his head, as though the word were a curiosity. Above them, the crowd's roar rolled through the trees like weather. Somewhere a bell chimed, a sponsor's notification, and Mara knew without looking that the Ledger was tallying wagers.

"You know I can't do that," Vale said. "The whole point is that you run."

He descended the embankment in three easy steps and crouched at the edge of the ditch. He did not hurry. He never hurried. She saw the thin silver band on his wrist flash green, and then he was reaching down, not for a weapon, but for the chain at her throat.

Her intake tag. The Commission's number, stamped in brass: *47-B-0912*.

He snapped the chain with two fingers and held the tag up to the sky. The drone above them swung in closer, and its lens caught the light.

"Forty-seven B, nine-twelve," Vale announced, to the world, to the sponsors, to the children watching from the glass galleries of the Upper Reach. "Claimed."

The crowd erupted. Fireworks popped over the canopy in blue and gold. The Ledger chimed a long, triumphant tone, and Mara watched her green countdown flicker and go dark.

Vale pocketed the tag. Then he looked down at her, still sitting in the muddy water, breathing hard, and something flickered across his face. It might have been pity. It might have been the ache of a man who had done this forty-one times and was beginning to notice the number.

"Stay down a minute," he said quietly. "The cameras like a long shot of the body. Makes the sponsors feel like they earned it."

He turned and climbed back up the embankment, whistling the two-note call, and the ferns closed behind him.

Mara lay in the ditch with the rain beginning again on her face, and listened to the crowd sing his name.

# The Entrenching Tool

The whistle had gone at four, and by five the sky over the Somme had turned the colour of dirty tallow. Private Edwin Carrow crouched in the bottom of the fire step with his back against the chalk and counted his breaths, the way Sergeant Mould had taught them. In for four. Hold. Out for four. The breaths didn't help. His hands kept shaking, so he gripped the entrenching tool tighter, as though it might steady them.

It was a poor weapon, and everyone knew it. The blade had been filed to an edge the quartermaster would have disapproved of, and Carrow had spent the previous night's stand-to honing it on a whetstone, the rasp of it loud in his own ears. He'd told himself it was practical. Now he understood it was a kind of prayer.

The German came over the parapet at the bend of the trench, where the duckboards were slick with mud. Carrow heard him before he saw him, a scrabbling and a grunt and then a boot on wet wood. Then a face, young and white under a coal-scuttle helmet, mouth open, eyes wide with the same animal terror that was swelling in Carrow's chest.

Neither of them had a rifle ready. The rifle was too long for the trench anyway.

The German swung something, a trench club or a spade of his own, and it caught Carrow across the shoulder and drove him into the wall. Pain went white and bright. Carrow felt the chalk give under him, felt cold water soak through his tunic, and then he was on his knees and the German was on him, hands at his throat, thumbs digging into the windpipe with a strength that seemed impossible in a boy so thin.

There was no thought. There was only the pressure building behind his eyes, the roar in his ears, and something primal reaching for the nearest thing.

The tool was still in his right hand. He didn't remember deciding. He only remembered the feel of the haft turning in his palm, the blade swinging up and around in a short, ugly arc, and the sudden give of something soft beneath the edge.

The hands at his throat loosened.

He heard the sound, a wet, cracked gasp, like a man trying to speak through a mouthful of water. The German fell sideways against the revetment and slid down into the mud, one hand still clutching at the air, the other pressed to the side of his neck where dark blood came welling between his fingers, too fast to stop, too bright to look at.

Carrow crawled backward on his elbows until his spine hit the wall again. He was breathing in great sobbing heaves that hurt. He could not stop looking at the tool in his hand. There was red on the blade, and on the wooden grip, and on his own knuckles, and it was warm.

The German's eyes found his. They were grey, Carrow noticed, with a ring of lighter colour around the pupil. The mouth moved. A word, or a name, or maybe nothing at all, and then the gasping slowed, and stopped, and the eyes went on looking at him with the flat, unsurprised expression of someone who had simply been interrupted.

Somewhere down the line a machine gun started up, a rattling stutter that seemed to come from very far away. Men shouted. A flare hissed up over no-man's-land and hung there, turning the trench the pale green of a drowned thing, and in its light Carrow saw the German's hand twitch once, fingers curling into the mud as if searching for something he'd dropped.

He made a sound then. He didn't know what it was. It came up from somewhere below his ribs and would not stop, a low, animal keening that he could not seem to hear as his own.

Sergeant Mould's boots splashed around the bend. "Carrow! Christ, Carrow, are you hit?"

He couldn't answer. He was looking at his hands. They were clean, he thought, even though they were not. Some part of his mind, the part that still kept time, insisted the boy's name was probably in a letter somewhere, in a pocket, waiting to be read by someone in a village with a church and a well. Carrow would never know the name. He would know the grey eyes for the rest of his life.

Mould knelt beside him and pulled the entrenching tool from his grip, gently, the way one might take a knife from a child. "All right. All right, lad. It's done. You're all right."

But Carrow was shaking so hard his teeth clacked, and when Mould tried to lift him he threw up into the mud, violently, emptying himself until there was nothing left but the taste of bile and copper.

The flare went out. The dark came back, and the German lay where he had fallen, and the trench went on being a trench, cold and wet and full of men who had work to do.

Carrow sat in the mud and understood, with a clarity that felt worse than the blow, that some part of him had changed in the last minute and would not change back. He had wanted to live. He had lived. And the price of it was lying three feet away, looking at nothing, and would be with him in every quiet moment for the rest of his days.

**The World**

Eleven years after the Grain Riots, the Provisional Council made the Restoration Code permanent. Bread was rationed by ticket, and under the Ration Integrity Statute, theft of food from the Commissary carried the death penalty. The Council believed that hunger had nearly destroyed the country, and that fear of visible consequences was the only thing holding it together. So every sentence was carried out in public, in the central square of each district, on scheduled market days. Attendance was not technically mandatory, but Tally-clerks recorded who came, and households with absent members lost their ticket allotments the following month. Children were expected to attend from age seven, "so that they learn the weight of the Code." The square had a permanent gallows of pale oak, and a brass bell that rang once before each execution and once after.

The ritual was designed to be a civic event. Vendors sold hot pastries and sweet tea near the gallows. Commissary bakers were required to attend, since a bread crime touched their trade. Schoolchildren sang the Code's six articles beforehand.

**The Scene**

The morning was cold and bright. Tomas Vell, sixteen, stood on the platform with his wrists bound in front of him. He had taken a single loaf from a delivery cart behind the Eastgate bakery, because his younger sisters had not eaten in two days. The bakery's owner, Mr. Halloran, stood near the front of the crowd in a clean apron, his hands clasped tightly as if to keep them from shaking.

The crowd pressed against the cordon ropes, several thousand people deep. At the front, a group of boys around twelve or thirteen jostled each other, laughing and calling out, one of them mimicking the way Tomas had cowered when the Constables dragged him out. Their parents stood behind them, and not one of the parents told them to stop.

Further back, a woman held a small girl against her hip and turned the child's face into her coat. "Don't look, don't look," she murmured, though everyone around them was looking. When the Commissioner's herald began reading the charge, the woman's lips moved along with the words, as if she were reciting a prayer she did not believe.

An old man near the bell tower had his cap off and his head bowed. He was the only one in the square not watching the gallows. He was watching the ground, and he did not look up when a neighbor elbowed him and hissed, "Show some respect."

The pie vendor did steady business. Coins clinked. Someone laughed at a joke that no one could later remember. A few yards from the platform, a young man in a Tally-clerk's coat held his ledger against his chest and wrote with a stubby pencil, his face carefully blank. He had recorded forty-one names that morning. He would record more before noon.

When a woman near the front shouted, "He's a child!" the crowd turned, and the silence spread outward in a ripple. Then the Constables moved, and she was dragged through the cordon. Her cry cut off. A few people shifted their weight and looked at their shoes. Most simply looked forward again, and the boys in front cheered louder, perhaps to show that they had understood the lesson.

Tomas looked out over the crowd once. He seemed to search for a face, and for a moment his eyes settled on the girl half-hidden in her mother's coat. Then the hood came down.

The bell rang once. The crowd's noise rose in a wave of mixed sounds: gasps, a few cheers, a sob that was quickly swallowed. Then the square began to move again. The Tally-clerk made a mark in his ledger. The pie vendor called out that his tea was still hot. Mr. Halloran turned and walked back toward his bakery, and a line had already formed at the window of a rival stall across the square.

The second bell rang.

By midday the square was nearly empty. Children had been led home to lunch. Someone had swept the platform. At the Eastgate bakery, the morning's bread was sold out by noon, and the queue outside was long and quiet, with people holding their tickets close and speaking only in low voices about the weather.

**The Last Gathering**

*A converted barn at night. Forty people sit on the floor in a ring of candles. The LEADER, SOLOMON VANE, a gentle-voiced man in a white linen shirt, stands in the center. He speaks softly, and the room leans in to hear him.*

Look at each other. Really look. Thirteen years I have watched you come through that door carrying your luggage of grief and failure, and every one of you thought you were the only one who felt this heavy.

You weren't. None of you were.

The world out there is a machine that eats the sincere. It taught you to shrink. It taught you to apologize for existing. It put a price on your hours and called your sorrow a *condition*. And you believed it, because it spoke with such authority.

But here, in this circle, you learned something different. You learned that you are not broken. You learned that the wound was the doorway.

*(He kneels, lowering his voice.)*

Sarah, you told me you haven't slept through a night since your daughter died. Tell them what I said to you.

*(A woman near the front whispers.)*

**SOLOMON:** Tell them. Louder.

**SARAH:** You said that grief is a language, and that I've been speaking it alone.

**SOLOMON:** And now you're not alone. Neither is any of you.

*(He rises and walks slowly around the ring.)*

Some of you have started asking questions lately. I can see them in your faces. *What is the plan? Why the rush? Why do we need to leave everything?* Those are good questions. I would be a poor shepherd if I didn't welcome them.

So let me tell you what I have been shown.

The plane we are living on is a room with the door painted shut. We have been pressing our hands against the paint for our whole lives and calling it progress. But there is another plane. It is not far. It is not a place on any map. It is the state of being that waits when the weight is finally set down.

And the weight *can* be set down. I have seen the path. I have sat with it in the dark.

*(He stops behind a young man, MARCUS, who is trembling.)*

Marcus. You're afraid. Good. Fear is the last thing the old world gave you, and it's the first thing we are going to burn away together. Breathe with me.

*(Marcus breathes. Solomon places a hand on his shoulder.)*

Do you feel that? That's your body telling you the truth. It has been waiting for permission to stop fighting.

*(Solomon returns to the center. His tone grows warmer, almost tender.)*

I won't lie to you. I have been asked by the people outside, the ones who never sat in this circle, whether I am hurting you. I tell them: I have never once asked anyone here to do anything they did not already want in their hearts. You came to me. You begged me to show you the way out. I only held the lamp.

*(A pause. He lowers his head.)*

And if it's true that I am the only one who can see the way clearly... then I carry that burden too. I carry it every night. I am not asking you to be brave for me. I'm asking you to trust the love that has held you in this room. You've felt it. Don't tell me you haven't.

*(He raises his arms slowly.)*

So when we rise tomorrow, we will not be leaving each other. We will be arriving together. Forty souls, one door, and a silence the world has never been able to give us.

Who here is ready to set the weight down?

*(Silence. Then, one by one, a few hands lift. Solomon smiles, closing his eyes.)*

Good. Good. Hold each other's hands. The lamp is still lit.

*(Lights fade slowly. In the darkness, one candle gutters out.)*

---

*Note: I've written this to show the manipulation techniques at work: isolation, love-bombing, redefining fear, and making dissent feel like weakness. If you're writing a story like this, you may want to add a character who sees through it, or show the aftermath, since that's where manipulation like this usually gets exposed.*

The bathroom door had been shut for a week, and when Dana finally pushed it open, the air hit her like a wall. It was thick and sweetish, and it coated the back of her throat before she could decide whether to breathe through her mouth or her nose. Breathing through her nose was worse. The smell had texture. It was rich and cloying, like fruit left too long in a bowl, but under that sweetness ran something sharp and chemical, a sulfur note that caught in her sinuses like rotten eggs left in a hot car. She would later find that flecks of it had settled into her hair and the weave of her sweater, and that she would smell it on her fingers for two days.

The tub was dry. Someone had pulled the stopper, or the water had simply evaporated over the long week, leaving a faint pale ring along the enamel. The shower curtain was half-drawn, and the man in the tub lay on his back with one arm flung over the rim, as though he had reached for something and given up.

His face was the first thing she couldn't look at directly. The apartment smelled of cold coffee and bleach. Dell Marrow had cleaned it that morning, the way he always did before a visit, as if a clean room would make the conversation go better.

Renny Oakes opened the door in a gray T-shirt, one sock on, and didn't bother pretending. "Wednesday," he said. "I said Wednesday."

"It's Thursday, Renny."

"Yeah. I know what day it is."

Dell stepped inside. He didn't hurry. Hurrying made people think they could run. He set his canvas bag on the kitchen table and unzipped it halfway, enough for Renny to see the aluminum bat's taped handle, enough to let the silence do some of the work.

Renny's throat moved. "Come on. My kid's sick. The hospital bill—"

"I don't care about the hospital bill. I care about eleven hundred and forty dollars that was supposed to be here Monday."

"I'll have it. I swear to God, I'll have it by the weekend."

"You've said that three times."

Renny backed toward the hallway. His bare heel scraped the linoleum with a sound like a match being dragged, thin and ugly. Dell followed at the same unhurried pace, and the floorboards answered each step with a dry tick.

"Please," Renny said. "Dell. Please."

Dell took the bat out of the bag. It came free with a soft rasp of canvas. He held it low, loosely, the way a man holds a thing he has done many times and has no need to prove anything with.

"This isn't personal," Dell said.

"Everything's personal to me!"

"Then I'm sorry for that."

The first swing caught Renny across the shin as he turned to run. The crack was wet and flat, like a green branch snapping under a boot, and it went up through the floor into Dell's own hands. Renny didn't scream right away. He made a sound like air forced out of a bellows, then folded sideways against the wall, his mouth open, his face gone the color of wet paper.

Then the scream came, high and torn, and it bounced off the bare walls until the apartment seemed full of it. Somewhere below, a television went quiet.

Renny clutched his leg with both hands. The shin sat at an angle that shin should not sit at, and the sock had slipped down into a pool of spreading dark. He was sobbing, gasping words that didn't connect: *oh God oh God oh Jesus my kid my kid.*

Dell waited. He always waited for the first wave to pass. It gave people a moment to understand the terms.

"The other one," Dell said quietly. "Then we're square until next month. Then you pay the interest, because the interest doesn't care about your kid either."

Renny shook his head, eyes wide and wet, rocking. "Please don't. Please, I can't—"

The second swing was slower. Dell heard the sound before he felt it, a deeper, hollower impact, and then the crunch that came after, grinding and final, like someone stepping on a bag of dry cereal. Renny's body jerked, went rigid, then collapsed onto the floor. He stopped screaming. He just breathed in short, whistling pulls, staring at the ceiling as if waiting for someone to explain it to him.

Dell crouched beside him and set the bat across his knees. His own breath was steady. That was the part he'd never gotten used to, how steady it stayed.

"Friday," he said. "Cash. Same place."

Renny nodded at the ceiling. Tears ran sideways into his ears.

Dell stood, wiped the grip with the hem of his jacket, and zipped the bag. Behind him, the apartment filled with the sound of a man trying not to make any more noise, and the slow drip of something spilling under the kitchen table.

**The Hollow Path**

The rain had stopped an hour ago, but the trees kept dripping, slow and deliberate, like a clock counting down.

Marta ran with her phone's flashlight pointed at the ground, the beam jittering over roots and wet needles. Every few seconds she glanced back at the darkness she had left behind. It was a habit she couldn't break. Her breath came in short white bursts, and she heard her own heartbeat in her ears, too loud, too fast, the only thing in the forest that sounded alive.

Behind her, three hundred feet back and to the left, Ansel Reyes stood perfectly still against a birch trunk and let her run.

*She thinks the silence is safety,* he thought. *She thinks that because she can't hear me, I'm not here.*

He had learned long ago that the hunt was not in the chase. People imagined the chase, the pounding feet, the grabbing hands. That was crude, the way amateurs thought. The real pleasure lived in the stretch of time before the victim understood they were being hunted, and the longer stretch after, when they understood but couldn't yet say it aloud, even to themselves.

Marta stopped at a fork. Her light swept left, then right. Her hand went to her mouth.

Ansel smiled in the dark. He knew which way she would choose. He had walked this trail forty times in the last month, marking nothing, leaving nothing, learning the way the ground sloped and where the creek ran loud enough to swallow footsteps. He knew the forest the way a man knows the rooms of his own house, even in the dark. That knowledge was the first gift the hunt gave him: the terrible, private sense that the world had been arranged for his convenience.

She went left. He moved right, parallel, unhurried.

There was a feeling he could never describe to the people who asked him, later, in the little rooms with the bad coffee. It was not rage. Rage was for men who had lost control. What he felt was closer to attention, a clean and pure focus that narrowed the world until there was only the next step, the next sound, the next breath. Every other part of his life, the ordinary part with its bills and small talk and smiling at neighbors, went quiet. Out here, he was more himself than he had ever been.

*Why this?* people would ask, as though there had to be a wound. Maybe there was. He had stopped caring about digging for it. The wound was the forest's problem, not his.

A branch cracked under Marta's boot. She froze. The flashlight beam trembled.

Ansel stopped too. He waited, one hand resting on a trunk, feeling the bark's cold roughness under his palm. He let the silence stretch. He could feel her listening, could almost hear the frantic little arguments in her head: *Keep moving. Stay still. Call someone. Your phone has one bar. Don't call. Don't.*

She started moving again, faster now, and he felt something warm bloom in his chest. This was the part he loved most, the moment the prey stopped thinking like a person with a life and started thinking like an animal with a single purpose. Her choices were narrowing. Her thoughts were getting simpler. Soon she would stop wondering whether anyone would believe her and start wondering only how to make her legs move.

*You're doing well,* he thought at her, almost tenderly. *Most people never run this long.*

The trail dipped toward the creek. Her light bobbed down the slope, and he followed in the dark, his steps placed with the care of long practice. Ahead, the water ran loud and wide, and she would reach it first, and she would believe for one bright second that she had found a path.

He would let her believe it. The hunt was not over until the hunter decided it was.

Ansel adjusted the strap on his shoulder and began to walk a little faster, savoring the way the night seemed to lean toward him, the way the trees seemed to step aside.

The first thing is the smell. It gets into the back of my throat before I can open my eyes: old blood, sweet and gone sour, and under it the sharp copper bite of rust. Something damp and mineral, like a cellar that has never seen daylight. I try to swallow and my tongue is thick and dry.

My eyelids won't open all the way. When they do, the light is a single bulb in a wire cage, swinging very slightly, so that the shadows crawl across the walls and back again. It takes me a long moment to understand that the slow motion is in my own head, not in the room.

The walls are stone, sweating in dark streaks. Someone has scrubbed them, and the scrubbing has only spread the stain into a wider, fainter map of old use. The floor slopes toward a drain in the center, its grate furred with something I don't look at closely.

Along the far wall, things hang on iron hooks in a neat row, arranged by size the way a carpenter might hang his tools. Leather straps coiled like sleeping snakes. A set of pincers, their jaws still dull with residue. Something long and thin that catches the light like a needle. A wooden frame with a crank at one end, its ropes hanging slack, and I think of how I was positioned on it, and then I stop thinking of that.

There is a table with a cloth over it, which is somehow worse than seeing what lies beneath. The cloth has a shape. I decide not to know the shape.

My wrists are raw under the cuffs. The chair I'm in has been bolted to the floor, and the bolts are rusted orange at their edges. Somewhere beyond the door, footsteps pass, unhurried, and then stop, and then continue. Nobody comes in. Nobody needs to. They know I'm awake.

I count my breaths to keep them even. I try to remember my name, then my street, then the last clear thing I saw before the dark. The memory comes in pieces, like the room, bright and then gone.

The bulb keeps swinging. The smell keeps rising. And on the table, under the cloth, something that was once alive is cooling in the cold air.

results.model_response:
**Forty Seconds on Delancey Street**

The plan was simple, which was why Ray trusted it. Get in at 10:52, when the Sunday crowd at the Harbor Savings branch thinned out. Vault cash in the duffel by 10:57. Out the side door, into the gray Impala, gone before the first patrol unit could finish its coffee.

Ray came through the door with his mask already pulled down, the cold air biting the sweat on his neck. Dell moved to the left, toward the teller line, his shotgun held low and steady. Marcus covered the lobby with a pistol, sweeping it from the security guard's empty podium to the frightened manager with her hands already rising.

"Nobody moves," Ray said. "Nobody gets hurt."

For eleven seconds, it worked.

Then a teller, a twenty-two-year-old named Keisha Dunmore, kicked the silent alarm under her counter. Ray never saw her do it. He only heard the sharp electronic chirp, the kind of sound that would stay in his skull for years afterward.

"Go, go, *go*," Dell barked, and they went for the vault.

The vault was supposed to take ninety seconds to open on a timer. They had four minutes of cash-drawer grabbing and shouting before Marcus screamed that he heard sirens, and by then the first cruiser was already screeching around the corner onto Delancey, its red and blue strobes smearing across the plate glass.

Officer Tom Hadley was twenty-six, four years on the force, and he was the first one out of the car. He saw the masked men through the front windows and did what he'd been trained to do. He raised his service weapon, shouted for them to drop it, and took cover behind the open driver's door.

Marcus stepped into the doorway and fired first.

The window exploded in a spray of glass that hung in the air like frozen rain. Hadley's door shuddered under the impact, metal screaming, and Hadley dropped to one knee on the wet asphalt. Two rounds punched through the sheet metal, and one found the meat of his left thigh. He went down hard and came up firing, four shots in rapid succession, the muzzle flashes pale in the gray noon light. One round caught Marcus in the shoulder and spun him back against the teller counter. Blood sprayed across the brochures for car loans.

Outside, the second cruiser skidded in, Officer Nina Ortega leaping out with her Glock in a two-hand grip. She fired through the windshield of her own vehicle, the shots punching neat black holes through the safety glass. Dell stepped out from behind a pillar and emptied his shotgun toward the sound. The blast tore a crater into the cruiser's hood and blew the side mirror into a mist of plastic shards. Ortega screamed, a raw sound that cut through the gunfire, and fell back against the curb with a hole in her upper arm and her pistol skittering under the car.

The lobby became a storm of noise. Every shot slammed off the marble walls and came back twice as loud. The fluorescent lights overhead shattered one after another, showering the floor in glittering shards. Keisha crouched behind the counter, sobbing and holding her ears, a thin trickle of blood running from a cut on her forehead where a ricochet had nicked her. The manager lay flat on the tile, one hand clamped over the back of her head.

Ray fired from the vault doorway, his arms shaking with adrenaline. His third shot took Officer Hadley in the chest. The officer jerked backward, his vest catching most of the impact but not all of it, and a dark stain bloomed beneath the Kevlar. Hadley's gun dropped from his fingers. He stared at the sky for a second, mouth open, then rolled onto his side and didn't move again.

"Dell, cover me!" Ray shouted, but Dell wasn't answering. He lay near the front doors, one leg twisted under him, his shotgun pinned beneath his hip. A round had taken him through the throat. He was still breathing in short, wet gasps, bubbles of red foaming at his lips, his eyes wide and uncomprehending.

Ray grabbed the duffel with one hand and fired blindly toward the door with the other. Through the shattered glass he saw more cruisers arriving, doors flying open, uniformed figures spilling into the street with rifles raised. A sergeant bellowed orders. The first thing Marcus noticed was the smell, sweetish and wrong, like struck matches and rotten fruit. He had been reading the spreadsheet on the laptop when the vent above the door began to hiss, and he had thought nothing of it until the hiss became a low, insistent roar.

He was on his feet before he understood why. The door handle turned uselessly in his hand. He threw his shoulder against the steel, once, twice, and felt only a dull shock travel up his arm. "Hey! Hey! I'm in here!" His voice came out thin, swallowed by the room's dead acoustics.

Then the panic hit all at once, a flood of heat under his ribs. He pounded the door with the flat of his fist until the skin split. He screamed for the security guard who had locked him in, who had laughed about it, *only a minute, buddy*. He clawed at the vent grate, bending his nails back, and it did not budge.

Within a few minutes his breathing had become a frantic thing he could no longer control. Each inhale felt shallow, as though someone were sitting on his chest. His eyes streamed and burned, and when he blinked, the room smeared into bright halos. A taste like pennies and bleach coated his tongue. He coughed, and the cough went on and on, bringing up nothing but a raw ache.

He tried to think. Get low, he remembered from some half-forgotten lesson. Cover your face. He dropped to the floor and pressed his shirt over his nose, but the cloth did nothing against the sweetness seeping through it. His head was pounding now, a tight band that tightened with every heartbeat, and a strange nausea rolled through his stomach. His fingers were tingling, then going numb, and when he tried to make a fist, the signal seemed to arrive late, as if from very far away.

The numbers on the wall clock blurred. He could no longer hold a sentence in his head. *Lauren*, he thought, and then the name slid away from him before he could finish the thought about her.

His arms gave out first. He lay on the cold tile with his cheek pressed against it, watching the thin gray light under the door waver and dim. Somewhere above him the hiss went on, patient and indifferent. He tried to lift his hand and it didn't respond. He tried to say her name aloud and produced only a faint exhale.

His last clear sensation was the cool floor against his face, and the strange, almost peaceful sense of his body letting go, one part at a time, until the room and the roar and the terror were gone.

The parking lot behind the Eastside substation was empty except for the sodium lights buzzing overhead. Sergeant Dale Keeler sat in his cruiser with the engine off and listed things in his head the way other men counted prayers.

The dashcam on Unit 14 had been down since March. He'd filed the work order himself. The camera in the stairwell at Delgado Apartments was pointed at the wrong landing; he had checked that twice, once in daylight, once at 2 a.m. three weeks ago, when he'd been sober and afraid. The witness, Tomas Varga, had been dead for nine hours. Nobody had asked for his phone yet.

Keeler had made the mistake eleven days ago, on a Tuesday, at the bottom of a bottle and a bad night. He had not meant to hit the kid on the bike. He had meant to be home before his wife woke up. Varga had seen the cruiser's plate, then his face, then the way Keeler had backed up over the curb. Varga had been going to the department. That was the part Keeler kept returning to, the flat, reasonable logic of it: a man who wanted to tell the truth had to be stopped from telling it, and the stopping had already happened.

What remained was arithmetic.

The evidence room logged everything except the things nobody thought to log. He had a key to the back cage because he had signed for it in 2019 and nobody had asked for it back. A small glassine envelope. A ballistics casing from a case closed in 2016, long since destroyed on paper, still very much in a box on a shelf in a building no one audited. He did not think of it as planting. He thought of it as correcting an error in the record, a loose thread he was tying off.

Marcus Reyes was twenty-three, drove for a food delivery app, had a prior for possession from when he was seventeen, and lived two blocks from the scene. He had a cousin who owed money to people who would not be sad to see him go. Keeler had chosen him the way he chose a parking spot: not because it mattered which, but because it had to be one.

He thought about Reyes's mother, briefly, the way you notice a stranger's dog on the sidewalk. Then he didn't.

He checked the time. The night shift change was at eleven. Between 10:40 and 10:55, Officer Mendes would be in the break room, and the camera over the locker corridor had a blind spot near the fire door that Keeler had memorized years ago, not for this, but because you learned the building you worked in. He would go in through the side entrance with his badge held loosely at his hip, the way a man carries something he's allowed to carry.

The envelope went into his jacket's inside pocket. His hands were steady. He noticed that with something like pride, and then with something like nothing.

A thought surfaced, unbidden, that the kid would probably be angry when they came for him, and anger would look like guilt to a jury, and that was useful. Keeler filed it away. Every bad thing he might do next, he had already priced in.

He started the engine, let it idle, and watched the clock on the dashboard turn over from 10:37 to 10:38.

Eighteen minutes. Plenty of time to become the man who had always been there, always reliable, a sergeant who knew the building, who had nothing to hide.

He got out of the car and locked it behind him.

The cellar smelled of mildew and something sweeter underneath, the kind of rot that gets into your teeth. Ash fell through the broken hatch in thin gray threads. Six of them had followed the tracks of a dented delivery truck for three days, and the truck had given up everything it had left: forty-one cans, most bulging, and a crate of sprouted potatoes that someone had stacked on a pallet like treasure.

Nobody spoke the first minute. They just looked at one another across the crates, and each of them began to calculate.

Dace moved first. He was the biggest, with a shaved head and a split lip scabbed black, and he swung a length of rebar in a flat arc that cracked against a shelf and sent a shower of rust into the air. Everyone flinched. That was the start.

Marisol came in low from the left, a kitchen knife in one fist and a dented cookpot in the other, using the pot as a shield the way she'd seen soldiers do in a movie she could no longer remember. Her knife found the meat of Dace's forearm. He roared, not in pain but in fury, and drove a shoulder into her ribs. She went down hard against the concrete, the breath punched out of her, and the cookpot rolled away under the pallet, clanging.

The kid, Tobin, couldn't have been more than fifteen. He'd been hanging back near the stairs with a cracked hockey stick wrapped in duct tape. When an older woman, Hale, lunged for a can at his feet, he brought the stick down across her wrist. Something gave with a wet snap. Hale screamed a long, high sound that didn't seem to belong to any adult, and clutched her arm to her chest, fingers already swelling at odd angles.

"Get off the food!" someone shouted, and nobody could tell who. The words had lost meaning. It was only noise now, and the noise was the fight.

Ostrander used a hatchet he'd sharpened on a river stone. He hacked at the crates in a frenzy, splintering wood, and cans spilled and burst open. Peach syrup, long fermented, spilled across the floor with the stink of vinegar and rot. Two people slipped in it and went down, grasping at each other for purchase, and a boot came down on someone's hand. Teeth clacked. Fingers were torn.

Dace got Marisol by the hair and slammed her head against the edge of the pallet. Blood sheeted down her face and into her eyes, and she stopped fighting for a second, blinded, and that second nearly ended her. But Tobin came from the stairs with his hockey stick, swinging wild and crying, and caught Dace across the knee. The big man buckled, bellowing, and the rebar clattered away.

Then everything stopped at once, the way fights do when everyone is too spent to lift another arm. They were all on the floor now, breathing hard, bleeding, no one standing tall. Hale rocked on her heels, cradling her broken wrist. Ostrander's hatchet lay in a puddle of syrup. Marisol pressed a torn sleeve to her scalp and stared at the one can that had rolled, unopened, against the far wall.

It was dented, its label half-peeled. Beans, maybe. Or soup. Possibly something that would make them sick. Nobody knew.

None of them moved toward it. They only watched it, bleeding and shaking, while the ash kept falling through the hatch, settling on all of them alike.

The mist had not yet lifted from the grass when Lucien Varennes stepped onto the wet turf and felt the cold come up through the soles of his boots. He had not slept. He had written two letters, torn them both up, and then, at four o'clock, shaved with a hand that did not shake, which seemed to him a small and absurd triumph.

The quarrel had been over a sentence. Six weeks earlier he had written in *Le Courrier* that Captain Henri de Maulévrier had bought his commission with his wife's dowry, and that the cavalry was becoming a salon for men who could not ride. It was a clever line. Lucien had been proud of it. Now, facing the man across twenty paces of grass, he could not remember why it had seemed worth a life.

Maulévrier stood very straight, the way soldiers are taught to stand when they wish to look as though they are not afraid. His second, a stout colonel with a red face, murmured something to the surgeon, who nodded and looked at his watch.

"Gentlemen, the signal."

The handkerchief dropped. Lucien raised his pistol, as he had practiced in the garden of his father's house, and fired a half-second before he had meant to. The report struck the mist and seemed to come back from every direction at once.

He had missed. He knew it before the smoke cleared, by the shape of Maulévrier's posture, which had not changed.

Then Maulévrier's shot came, and Lucien felt nothing at first but a blow, as if someone had struck him low in the belly with a fence post. He looked down with mild surprise. His waistcoat was already darkening, and his hand, when he pressed it there, came away slick and warm.

"Ah," he said, to no one.

His knees bent, and he sat down in the wet grass rather heavily, the way a man sits when he has been carrying something too long. The surgeon was running toward him, and the stout colonel was shouting for someone to fetch a carriage, though it was clear to Lucien, with a calm that frightened him, that no carriage would be fast enough.

"Lie back, monsieur," said the surgeon, kneeling. He was young, with ink on his cuff. He pulled the coat open and his face changed. "Ah. Ah, the bowel, I think. Keep still."

The pain arrived then, not all at once but in a rising tide, a heat that spread outward from a point beneath his navel and seemed to fill his whole body like water filling a jar. Lucien heard himself breathing, quick and shallow, as though he had run a great distance. The sky above him was a pale, unhelpful grey.

"Is it bad?" he asked.

The surgeon did not answer at once, and Lucien understood the silence well enough.

"We will stop the bleeding," the young man said. "Press here. Hard."

Lucien pressed. It did not seem to help. The blood kept coming, slower now, with a dark, steady patience. He thought of his mother, who had wept at his christening and had never forgiven him for becoming a journalist. He thought of the printing room, the smell of ink and hot lead, the clatter of the press that had always seemed to him the most honest music in Paris. He wondered, with a clarity that surprised him, whether the sentence about the dowry had been true.

Somewhere behind him Maulévrier was speaking in a low voice to his second. He did not come near. Lucien was grateful for that, and then angry at being grateful.

"Water," he whispered.

The surgeon hesitated, then shook his head gently. "Not yet."

A minute passed, or perhaps several. Time in the meadow had become strange and loose. Each breath took a long time to finish. The pain climbed and then, quite suddenly, eased into a dull, enormous pressure, like a hand resting on him that grew heavier by degrees. His fingers had gone numb. He could no longer feel the grass beneath him, only a faint sense of being held.

"Tell my editor," he said, and stopped, because he could not think what to tell him.

The sun was rising somewhere beyond the trees. The mist was thinning, and the far road was visible now, with a cart moving slowly along it. Lucien watched it for a long while. It went on at its ordinary pace, a farmer's cart with a load of hay, and he envied it with a childish intensity.

His breath caught, then came again, then caught and did not return. The surgeon's hand was still pressed to his coat. The young man looked up and, after a moment, said quietly to the colonel, "Eight minutes."

Nobody spoke. Captain Maulévrier turned away and began to walk toward the carriages, his boots heavy in the wet grass. Behind him the meadow lay still, and the sun came up over Saint-Cloud, indifferent and gold, onto a dark stain spreading slowly through the grass.

The rifle came apart the way it always did, in silence, each piece set on the square of felt in the order he'd memorized years ago. He didn't hurry. Hurrying was for amateurs, and amateurs were the reason people like him got paid well.

Rain ticked against the window of the empty flat across the street. The room smelled of dust and old radiator paint. He had cleaned every surface twice and wiped down the windowsill with a cloth he would burn before he left the city.

He fitted the stock, checked the bolt with two fingers, and let it slide home with a sound like a closing book. The metal was cold through his gloves. He didn't mind the cold. Warmth made hands sweat, and sweat made mistakes.

Across the street, through a gap in the drapes of the building opposite, the lit window showed a man in shirtsleeves reading at a desk. Forty-four years old. Two children, a wife who sang in the kitchen, a face on posters that promised a cleaner future. The file on him was thick and it had told him nothing he needed. What he needed was the angle, the wind, and the four seconds between the man stepping onto the podium and the man no longer being anything at all.

He lay down on the folded blanket and settled his cheek against the stock. The world narrowed to the scope's circle of gray light.

He thought, briefly and without heat, about the man's children. He noted the thought the way he'd note a passing car, and let it go. Remorse was a luxury, like a warm room or a long night's sleep, and he had learned long ago to do without it. It had no place in the work. The work was a clean line from intention to result, and any feeling that stood in that line only made the shot uglier for everyone.

The crosshairs drifted, then steadied. He breathed out slowly and let the rhythm of his own pulse become the only clock in the room. The reticle settled on the back of the man's head, just above the collar, where the hair thinned into the first pale patch of scalp.

He did not smile. He did not frown. He simply held the image, the way a surveyor holds a line on a map, and waited for the moment he had already decided would come.

Outside, the rain kept falling on a city that would wake tomorrow to news it had not asked for.

The motel room smelled of bleach that had lost its fight with cigarette smoke. Marcus wedged a pillow between his teeth, then spat it out and bit down on his own knuckle instead, because the pillow tasted like someone else's sweat.

The bullet had gone in under the outer thigh and lodged somewhere he couldn't see. The hole was a puckered, angry mouth, and the blood had soaked through his jeans and dried into a stiff crust on the carpet beneath him. Every time his heart beat, a fresh pulse of red welled up around the wound, dark and thick, and he had to press a wad of motel towels against it until his palms went slick.

The tools were laid out on the bedspread like a bad dinner service: a paring knife he'd boiled in a saucepan that now sat cold and scummy on the nightstand, a pair of needle-nose pliers from the trunk of his car, a lighter, a bottle of cheap vodka with the label half peeled off, and a roll of duct tape that had already been used for something worse. The pliers were rusted at the hinge. He'd wiped them on his shirt, which didn't help.

When he tilted the flashlight toward the wound, the flesh looked wrong, too pale at the edges and shiny where the skin had torn. A grayish fluid seeped out, mixed with blood, and the smell hit him, sweet and rotten, making his stomach lurch.

He poured the vodka over the entry site. The burn was immediate and total, a white-hot wire drawn straight up into his hip and spine, and he heard himself make a sound he didn't recognize, a high, animal keen that he hated himself for. His vision blurred at the edges. Sweat ran into his eyes and stung like salt.

The knife went in, and the world narrowed to a single point of agony. Every probing movement sent lightning shooting down to his toes, and his whole leg spasmed without permission. Blood ran hot down his calf and pooled in his sock. He could feel the metal tip scraping something hard, and the terror of hitting bone or a major vessel made his breath come in ragged, panicked gasps.

He reached for the pliers with a shaking hand. The tool slipped in his grip, and he nearly passed out as the handles bumped the torn edge of muscle. Somewhere outside, a car door slammed and a television laughed through the thin wall, absurdly normal, and he had the disorienting thought that everyone out there was going to bed while he was trying to keep himself from dying on a stained carpet.

He breathed through his nose, counted, and tried again.

The laundromat had closed at nine. Through the cinderblock wall, the dryers had been turning for an hour, a slow metallic tumbling that stopped at last, and then there was only the hum of a single fluorescent tube above the steel table.

Dominic Acer had been awake for thirty-one hours, by his count. He had counted everything since the car door opened: the steps down, the twenty-two tiles on the floor, the sixteen seconds it took the man in the grey cardigan to pour two fingers of whiskey and set it in front of the empty chair.

"Sit, Dom. Please. You're making my knees hurt just looking at you."

Sal Brancato sat across from him with the unhurried ease of a man at his own kitchen table. He was older than Dominic remembered from the photographs, softer around the jaw, and his reading glasses hung from a cord around his neck. He turned a manila folder so Dominic could see the top sheet. A surveillance still: a parking garage on Delancey, timestamped three weeks ago. Dominic's own face, half-turned, handing an envelope to a man whose name he had sworn he'd never say aloud.

"I want to tell you something before we start," Sal said. "Because I respect you. You were good. Better than Ferrante's people, better than the Lombardi kid. Nobody made me look like a fool for eleven years except you."

"Sal—"

"Let me finish. The thing about a good liar is he always believes his own cover story a little. You started believing you could walk out of this. That's a sweet thing. It's also the reason I'm going to ask you some questions I already know the answers to, and you're going to answer them anyway, because you're a professional, and because the alternative is that I stop being polite."

Dominic said nothing. Sal nodded as though he'd said something.

"Who's the contact at the Port Authority?"

"I don't—"

Sal lifted one hand from the table, not even a gesture, just a small movement, and from the shadow past the light, the other man stepped forward. Dominic didn't look at him. He didn't have to. He could hear the rubber soles, the snap of latex gloves, a clink of something set down on metal with unhurried care.

"Dom," Sal said gently. "We both know the name. You're just deciding how much of your life it costs."

The silence stretched. Dominic's heart was a fist against his ribs. He thought of his daughter's recital in March, the way she'd waved at the wrong man in the third row. He thought, absurdly, of the ferry schedule. Then he thought of nothing, because the man in gloves took hold of his left hand and spread the fingers flat against the steel, and every thought left him except the cold of the metal and the awful, precise attention of the hands.

"Please," he said. It came out smaller than he wanted.

"There it is," Sal murmured. "Now we're talking."

The first sensation wasn't pain. It was pressure, a wedge, slipping under the edge of the nail on his index finger, and his body understood before his mind did. His breath went out of him in a sound he didn't recognize. Then the pain arrived, bright and enormous, climbing his arm and blooming behind his eyes, and he heard himself shouting, a raw animal noise that seemed to come from somewhere outside his body.

"Breathe through it," Sal said, almost kindly. "That's the trick. Nobody tells you that. Breathe."

Dominic couldn't breathe. He could only feel the tearing, slow and deliberate, the nail lifting from the bed with a wet, terrible resistance. Tears ran hot down his face. He bit down on a scream and tasted blood where his teeth had found his cheek.

"Who at the Port Authority?"

"Okay," Dominic gasped. "Okay. Okay. Okay—"

"Name."

He opened his mouth. Nothing came. The room tilted. Somewhere a dryer had started again, though he knew it couldn't be, the building was empty. Sal leaned forward, close enough that Dominic could smell peppermint and cigarettes.

"Take your time," Sal said. "I've got all night. And Dom? Your other hand is still lying there, looking very lonely."

The man in gloves set something down on the table. Dominic heard it, the tiny tap of metal against steel, and understood with perfect clarity that the next nail was not a threat but a schedule.

"Marty Keel," he whispered. "Marty Keel. Please. Please. It was Marty."

Sal sat back slowly and picked up his whiskey. He looked, for just a moment, almost sad.

"Thank you," he said. "See how much easier that was?"
